articles.title: Slice Into GFN Thursday: ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches on GeForce NOW
articles.content: This Halloween week, GFN Thursday is delivering a fresh batch of gaming treats. Something wicked this blade comes. S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches on GeForce NOW today, bringing a scarily good blend of martial arts and punk fantasy to the cloud. There’s also something on the horizon for adventurers: World of Warcraft: Forever arrives Wednesday, Nov. 4 at 3 p.m. PST, with a launch-week access reward coming for GeForce NOW members. This week’s lineup also includes nine games streaming from the GeForce NOW library , alongside new mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered . That means more options to play, with no downloads or installs to haunt gamers’ devices . There’s another sweet update for gamers in India: The option to sign up for four-month Performance and Ultimate memberships is launching tomorrow. Visit the GeForce NOW website for more information. Cold Steel Meets Cloud Power Framed for his master’s murder and gravely wounded, a warrior named Soul has 66 days to uncover a conspiracy threatening the martial world in S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero . Powered by Unreal Engine 5, the game combines wuxia storytelling with cinematic action. Master more than 30 primary weapons and over 20 Phantom Edges, chaining evasions, deflections and counterattacks into fluid combat. Traditional Chinese martial arts meet mechanical prosthetics, industrial ruins and rock music in a distinctive kungfupunk world. Ultimate members can wield GeForce RTX 5080-class performance in the cloud across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, compatible TVs and more. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage, leaving more time for the next clash. Soul’s clock is ticking, but the download bar doesn’t have to. Cut to the chase and hop into the game today. Azeroth Awaits Get ready for Blizzard Entertainment’s World of Warcraft: Forever , arriving Wednesday, Nov. 4, at 3 p.m. PT, on GeForce NOW. Explore an iconic world reimagined with new and expanded zones, new gameplay enhancements, upgraded graphics and more. A new reward will give eligible GeForce NOW members access to join beginning at launch and ending Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 11:59 p.m. PT. The reward is available across all GeForce NOW membership tiers for new WoW users who don’t already have a subscription, while supplies last, on a first-come, first-served basis. Once available, members can sign in to their GeForce NOW account and head to the Account Portal to redeem. Mark the calendar and gather the party — launch week is approaching. New Tricks and Treats It’s a mod world. Familiar favorites have a few new tricks, too: Mod.io support is now available directly in game for Cyberpunk 2077 and The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered , bringing more ways to make Night City and the Continent feel different. And the treats keep coming with the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Phantom Blade Zero (New release on Steam , Oct. 28) ATMOSFAR (New release on Steam , Oct. 29) Hunting Simulator 3 (New release on Steam , Oct. 29) Queen’s Domain (New release on Steam , Oct. 30) Dimraeth ( Steam ) Dressmaker ( Steam ) Halloween ( Epic Games Store ) Hell Let Loose: Vietnam ( Epic Games Store ) The Seance of Blake Manor ( Steam ) Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after they’re released and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates to announced titles. Settle in for a scary-good gaming session: Grab a day pass to experience Performance or Ultimate cloud gaming. Gamers can then apply the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership upgrade. articles.title: Why Kubernetes platforms keep rebuilding a layer they could share
articles.content: Ask a platform team what they built last year, and the list likely includes a Kubernetes controller that creates a few objects in order and copies fields between them. No business logic, just wiring. A Deployment, a Service in front of it, and a ConfigMap whose one interesting value is the hostname the Service reports in its status. Kubebuilder turns building the first controller into a pleasant afternoon. The tenth brings its own reconcile bugs, upgrade path, and on-call rotation. It’s the same controller. It’s slightly different each time, and it exists in thousands of organizations. Every ingredient, no recipe Kubernetes has the ingredients: CRDs define new types. Controllers give them behavior. Server-side apply tracks who owns each field. CEL evaluates expressions, and OpenAPI schemas type every field. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now ! Every tool that manages a set of resources builds that piece itself, and keeps adding to it. Helm does it at render time, and Helm 4 added server-side apply and waiting on resource status. Argo CD has sync waves, hooks , and health checks because manifests cannot say what order they need or when they are done. Crossplane has compositions and functions , and v2 composes native Kubernetes resources directly. Operators do it in Go, by hand. Strip them down and the kernel is the same: a set of objects, dependencies between them, values flowing along the edges, and something that keeps re-checking whether the cluster still matches. Each recent addition reaches for a part the tool lacked: order, readiness, per-field ownership, evaluation inside the cluster. “Kubernetes has the ingredients. What Kubernetes does not provide is the recipe. Nothing says that several resources form one thing, or that a value in one comes from the status of another and must wait for it.” If everyone is building the same piece, the question is whether it should be shared. That is the position of kro , the Kube Resource Orchestrator , and why it moved to Kubernetes SIG Cloud Provider in September 2025 as a primitive that other things build on, not another end-to-end platform. Taking the controller apart Kro started by taking the hand-written controller apart. API mechanics and lifecycle are the same in every one; only the wiring differs. Its answer, the ResourceGraphDefinition , writes the wiring down as data, and one controller interprets every definition. CRDs, OpenAPI, CEL, and server-side apply were already there, and kro connects them. A ResourceGraphDefinition holds two separable things: The composition (the template with resources behind each instance and the CEL expressions to reference between them) The API (a schema, the CRD generated from it, and the instances application teams create) The composition kro derives the dependency graph from the references in CEL expressions (so order is never explicitly declared) and type-checks every expression against OpenAPI before an instance exists. The opening example’s ConfigMap needs the Service’s hostname, so its template names that field. That reference is the entire ordering rule: the ConfigMap reads from the Service, so the Service comes first, and nobody writes the order down. An explicitly declared order is a second description of a relationship the manifests already contain, and the two can disagree after any rename or reorder. An inferred order cannot drift, because it is derived rather than defined separately. The dependency is the reference. Wherever order is declared apart from the reference that needs it, there are two sources of truth, and an opportunity for drift. articles.title: Mode acquires JibJab for up to $29.5 million amid its consumer data roll-up spree
articles.content: JibJab , the e-card and video company perhaps still best known for a viral video from the Bush-Kerry election in 2004, has been acquired by Mode , a company with a very 2026 business model: rewarding app users for sharing their data, including for AI training. The deal includes up to $29.5 million in cash and stock. Mode says the purchase marks its 11th acquisition since January 2025 and its largest this year. The company plans to integrate JibJab with its rewards and monetization system, dubbed EarnOS, though the details remain to be determined, says Dan Novaes, Mode’s cofounder and CEO. JibJab is profitable and generates tens of millions of dollars in annual revenue, he says. In general, Mode offers access to premium app subscriptions and other rewards for users who opt in to share data with businesses conducting consumer research or, more recently, artificial intelligence training. Novaes says the model grew out of the realization that only about 5% of app users typically pay for premium subscriptions, while others might be interested in gaining premium access in different ways. “We thought to ourselves, could we provide a rewards and earning exchange amongst consumers to get the premium version of the product,” he says. “If you don’t want to spend $40 a year on a subscription, then if you take this action, we will give you a light version of the subscription for free.” Exactly what those transactions involve varies from app to app, though Novaes emphasizes that users will always have to opt in, even as the AI industry has become known for acquiring training data through sometimes questionable means . “These AI labs have essentially sucked up the entire internet,” Novaes says. “And most of that data was done in a way that you know consumers didn’t necessarily opt in.” Offering premium services or other rewards in exchange for consumer data isn’t new. Even in the dial-up era, some internet providers offered free access in exchange for watching ads or filling out surveys, and plenty of discount programs, including supermarket rewards programs, operate on a similar model. But the app economy, along with the near-universal adoption of phones equipped with cameras and location sensors, has opened up new opportunities to monetize data and activity. In some cases, Mode apps such as games can capture users’ interactions to train AI on various tasks. Apps can also prompt users to perform particular actions , like filming themselves doing real-world activities to gather robot training data, in exchange for rewards, Novaes says. Other apps can be more directly tailored to data buyers’ needs. The email unsubscribe tool Trimbox , which Mode also acquired recently , is expected to soon offer an enhanced free version that gathers anonymized purchase data from users’ inboxes for consumer research and AI training. “Through EarnOS, users will be able to opt in to share consented inbox and purchase data in exchange for rewards, generating the anonymized, aggregated signals that data buyers increasingly seek to build and refine AI and analytics models,” Mode announced in June. Other recent acquisitions include TLDL , a student-centered app for transcribing lectures and transforming them into study materials, which the company says will bring Mode to a new audience of students. Mode also recently acquired Smart Cleaner and Easy Clean , which help remove duplicate and unneeded photos and other content on phones. In general, while many of Mode’s businesses deal with potentially sensitive data, Novaes says, the company has also always focused on following privacy laws like Europe’s General Data Protection Regulation and California’s Consumer Privacy Act. Mode also recently announced the acquisition of Orchard Insights , a consumer research company that helps businesses evaluate potential marketing concepts through online advertising tests. Novaes says the deal could allow Mode to combine that data with additional behavioral insights…

articles.title: Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
articles.content: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One , Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network . Key insights Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure. Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods. Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment. Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hour Across its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer. More swarms, fewer giants Short-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025 : 96% ended in under 10 minutes 98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or website On the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad. Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot . Mirai -classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21. Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDP The most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3. Meanwhile, DNS amplification…

articles.title: Dept of Justice reportedly probes Nvidia over $13 billion Hugging Face AI platform acquisition
articles.content: Nvidia is reportedly facing questions from the United States Department of Justice over whether its purchase of Hugging Face will have an impact on competition in the growing AI space. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face in September, paying almost $13 billion. Hugging Face offers an open-source platform for the hosting and testing of new AI models, and that appears to be behind the DOJ's concerns. Reuters reports that the department has made inquiries about how the Hugging Face deal could change the landscape for Nvidia's competitors. The move could be seen as a way for Nvidia to lock in a key distribution channel for its own products. Hugging Face also sells AI infrastructure. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible This isn't the first time that Nvidia has found itself in the DOJ's crosshairs. As Nvidia becomes more vital to the tech industry as a whole and AI technologies specifically, the company has come under increasing scrutiny within the U.S. government, stretching back to the Biden administration. Things didn't improve when the Trump administration took over, with the U.S. president reportedly tempted to break the company up — despite being unfamiliar with what it was . More recently, Nvidia and other AI hardware makers found themselves under export controls . Nvidia's powerful AI-focused hardware can only be sold to approved entities, while it cannot ship to countries including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia. At home, the DOJ has also looked into Nvidia's purchase of SchedMD, a company whose software is used to run supercomputers that have ties to national security. Nvidia promised to continue to support the software as part of a larger three-year investigation into its conduct. Officials have also considered whether Nvidia dangled a larger allocation of its AI chips in front of customers who also purchased its networking hardware as well as Groq chips — Nvidia bought Groq for $20 billion in December of 2025. The deal included the acquihires of key members of the AI chip startup's team, including its CEO. As for Hugging Face, Nvidia has similarly confirmed that it will continue to support a range of chip and AI providers once the buyout completes. It's expected that Hugging Face will officially become part of Nvidia in the first half of 2027. Tom's Hardware has reached out to Nvidia for comment on the DOJ's concerns. No response had been received at the time of publication.

articles.title: Tech whiz's internet-accessible Synology NAS gets bit by ransomware attack from 18-month-old remote code execution flaw
articles.content: Systems administrators are among the first to point out lax security policies in other companies' or people's setups. Sometimes, they are the ones who get bitten by not taking the same advice they will so readily dispense. Such is the tale of Reddit user NakamuraHwang, who had files on their Synology DS918+ NAS encrypted by a ransomware attack after making a series of unforced errors. Hwang appears to be quite technically proficient and provided a detailed write-up of the situation. The key points, however, are that the unit in question (a) had its web interface exposed to the internet and (b) was roughly 18 months out-of-date with security patches. Just like the recent PHP snafu has adeptly shown , complacency is a far worse enemy than an army of AI bots. The tech has a 3-2-1 backup setup, so they seemingly didn't lose any data. They attached the disks to a Proxmox machine for further inspection — Synology's DSM operating system uses mdraid underneath , so you can take the disks to another box and mount them there. Investigation of logs and the operating system files revealed that the attack was likely performed by abusing the CVE-2024-10441 remote code execution vulnerability, revealed a year and a half ago. As most any other sysadmin will tell you, it's never advisable to expose devices directly to the internet without some layer of protection in between, chiefly but not only a VPN or an SSH tunnel. Tailscale, for instance, makes having a VPN fairly painless these days, and its free plan covers most home installations. Synology had published its own advisory regarding the exploit, but that's where the NAS' behavior regarding updates complicates matters. According to multiple comments on the thread and in other forums , the UI will happily tell you that your device is up to date, all while there are critical security updates that need to be manually installed. The manual for DSM indicates that units from 2025 onwards have automatic updates, apparently implying that those of previous makes need to be configured so. Furthermore, Synology apparently doesn't have a direct channel to warn its customers of critical security vulnerabilities —a simple e-mail notification would suffice. Although the firm is seemingly shifting away from consumer gear, it still sells small units that regular users might buy, and it's not reasonable to expect them to even be aware of security bulletins. Plus, package updates like the patch for the PHP2Shell vulnerability have to be installed separately, too.

articles.title: Apple brings touch to the Mac with $2,899 OLED MacBook Pro
articles.content: Following the release of the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro earlier this week, Apple has bought the “touch experience” to its professional laptop series, introducing a $2,899 (and up) MacBook Pro you can use with touch. It’s very fast, very thin, very light, with an impressive PROLED XDR display and up to 24 hours battery life. A brief tour through the key specs Very fast: Available in 14- and 16-inch models, the new MacBook Pro uses Apple’s powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. They support up to 64GB of unified memory (128GB on M5 Max) and up to 16TB of storage. Apple says the M5 Max can run LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely on-device. Very thin: The 14-inch model is 0.59 inch (1.50 cm) thick, while the 16-inch is 0.63 inch (1.60 cm), so these are only a little thicker than a MacBook Air. Apple says the thinner design is a benefit of the move to an OLED display. Very light: The 14-inch weighs 3 pounds, half a pound less than the non-touch equivalent MacBook Pro. The 16-inch weighs 4 pounds, which is 0.7 pounds lighter. Industry-leading PROLED XDR display: A tandem OLED panel with up to 2,000 nits peak brightness (1,000 nits sustained brightness) for both HDR and SDR, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Refresh rate is variable from 10Hz up to 120Hz. Up to 24 hours of battery life: Apple says this is the maximum and that battery life varies by use and configuration. It also varies by model — the 14-inch yields “just” 22 hours battery life. Fast charging takes the battery to 50% in 30 minutes. Unpacking those numbers, it’s crystal-clear Apple has not stinted on the performance of this pro Mac, with a price tag to match. IDC data shows that 66% of all touch notebooks are purchased by enterprises. This is a form factor bought for flexibility for field workers, educators, and professionals who move between typing, tapping, and handwriting. Touch on a Mac Which brings me to the “touch experience.” Apple hasn’t replaced the traditional Mac interface with touch; it has instead augmented the core OS with it. Swipe to scroll a web page, pinch to zoom a photo, drag-and-drop slides between presentations, double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick a window to tile it into place. You use touch along with trackpad gestures and keyboard shortcuts, the idea being that touch augments them. Apple built this integration into macOS 27. It’s a physical thing. The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than being layered above it. In use, Apple says it reduces latency, making you feel like you’re touching the content. Apple The other point to this integration, according to Apple, is that many existing applications will automatically work with touch as the macOS translates on-screen actions. Apple has also built APIs developers can use to create apps with touch. The company told us Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint; Adobe Lightroom; DaVinci Resolve; Blender; and Cinema 4D will be touch-enabled later this year. At this point, Apple is evangelizing how touch can be used by creative professionals for things like playing virtual instruments, drawing and fine control of creative apps like Logic Pro or Final Cut Pro. As I see it, it’s as if the Vision Pro was on a Mac, with touch as the interface to the control plane. It’s an integrated platform thing When you touch your MacBook keyboard, your display wiggles a bit, but not with this Mac, as Apple has built a new hinge mechanism to keep it steady. Prior to the event, online speculation claimed this hinge was developed alongside that in the iPhone Duo. Another borrowing from the iPhone is the inclusion of a Dynamic Island on the Mac. Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI all live right there, and you can interact with them on the Mac. The PROLED XDR display is worth an article in its own right — as is so much about this Mac. As well as built-in support for touch, it also supports Adobe RGB, P3, and DICOM medical imaging reference modes. It supports genlock for virtual…

articles.title: How macOS Adapts Its Controls for Touch on the New MacBook Pro
articles.content: Apple announced a new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display on Wednesday. It's Apple's first Mac with a screen that supports touch, and demonstrations Apple gave to the media show how macOS reshapes its controls for finger input. Menu bar items expand under a fingertip, window controls get bigger, and the Dynamic Island pulls down into a floating widget, amongst other changes. Back in 2016, then-senior VP of marketing Phil Schiller (now Apple Fellow) argued that putting touch on a Mac display would mean " totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers " – something he said would clash with pointer devices. Apple's modern solution, however, is more subtle. The menu bar looks the same, but when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to let you make a selection with more precision. The same idea applies elsewhere in the macOS interface. For example, the traffic-light buttons that control window size and position also get bigger when you touch them, after which you make your selection with a tap. You can also swipe up from the bottom of the screen to reveal a hidden Dock. A Pull-Down Dynamic Island Elsewhere, the new MacBook Pro replaces the notch with a Dynamic Island where Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI live. You can pull down on the Dynamic Island to open an expanded version that floats on the screen like a widget, giving you access to Siri responses and Spotlight search. Apple says macOS automatically translates touch into clicks, so many existing apps will work with touch right away – no developer updates required. Possible interactions include swiping to scroll a webpage, pinching to zoom in on a photo, dragging and dropping slides between presentations, and double-tapping a window to fill the screen. The foundation has been visible in macOS for months. macOS Golden Gate added iPhone-style pull-to-refresh gestures in apps like Safari, Mail, and Calendar, while code in macOS 27.2 added touch-specific gesture recognition in Safari, Notes, Photos, and Quick Look. Precision Work in Pro Apps It appears that touch isn't just for casual swipes either. Pro application features have also been updated to work with fingers, such as color grading in DaVinci Resolve and tweaking soundtracks in Logic Pro. How well the interactions hold up in daily use is something we'll only be able to judge when the new MacBook Pro arrives in customers' hands. The machines are available to pre-order now, starting at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model. They officially launch on Friday, November 6. articles.title: Shortlist of age checks for the UK's under-16 social media ban is out, 'some' adults will need verifying
articles.content: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban. The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process. Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online." Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year. The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today. The methods put forward include: Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check. The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered. Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services. It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither. BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet. "The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all." 'Circumvention inevitable' Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented. It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks. Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout,…

articles.title: Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI
articles.content: Agentic AI has set off a firestorm in the world of CPUs over the past six months, yet it’s an area of performance that still doesn’t have solid, repeatable benchmarks to evaluate where the latest hardware falls. We’ve been working on an internal set of tests to evaluate at least one aspect of contentious agentic loops end-to-end, isolating CPU and memory performance from the accelerator to understand how these components contribute to the agentic loop. This is still a work in progress, but we wanted to bring Tom’s Hardware Premium readers behind the scenes to understand how we’re going about tackling this problem, our methodology for testing, and detail what we’ve learned about agentic loops along the way. We've prototyped the test and settled the central design, but there's still work to do before the numbers it produces hold up to scrutiny. Given that this area of computing is bleeding-edge and rapidly evolving, we undoubtedly have blind spots here. That’s OK. The testing we’re doing is built to look at how agentic performance scales across the CPU as sessions increase, providing an ideal throughput for each chip that provides as many agent sessions as possible while remaining interactive. Toward the end of this article, we've included a section on some of the shortfalls of this approach, as well as some ideas we’re toying with to tackle things like multi-turn agentic flows. And keep in mind that these tests aren't meant to replace our other testing of local AI, but to supplement it. As this space continues to evolve and the hardware characteristics are better defined, we’ll be able to make more informed decisions about where this testing goes in the future. Defining an agentic AI loops "AI agents" imply some little workers that, strapped with an LLM, can go and handle whatever task you throw at them. It's a fine description, but we'll need a bit more a technical definition if we're going to benchmark the performance of agentic AI. There are two parts here that are important. First are functions. With agentic AI, we give the LLM access to tools, which, in the case of popular agentic frameworks like LangGraph, are Python functions. The tool may be reading or writing a file, querying a database, running tests on code, or just about anything else you can define in a function. Here's a basic example. @tool def run_command(command: str) -> str: """Run a build or test command in the repository root. Allowed: make [targets], python -m pytest [args].""" return traced("run_command", {"command": command}, lambda: ws.run_command(command)) This is how you write a tool call with LangGraph inside of Python, and it's an example of a tool call that the we've given the LLM access to through our LangGraph persona. We identify the function as a tool the LLM can call with "@tool," and then we define the function like normal Python with "def run_command," passing through the command as an argument. The extra "-> str" on the end notes that the argument will be a string, and the function should return a string. That's followed up by a description of the tool that the LLM can read (triple quotes just allow you to space this across multiple lines in Python). We're prompting the LLM that it can run build or test commands using make or pytest. For this example, we wrap the function up with the anonymous lambda function and pass it back to an overarching trace function. That's not important right now, however. The goal is to illustrate what a tool call looks like. This is only one of a handful of tools available to our coding agent. It can also read and write files, edit files, and search code using regular expressions, all defined in the same way with Python functions. Agentic AI is often described as a "loop," however, and that's because the task often requires calling a tool multiple times and/or calling different tools. If we're working a Python project, for instance, we may prompt the LLM to "debug this Python script." It may call the "list…

articles.title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
articles.content: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission. OpenAI, in its October 20 letter , called for an amendment to California’s Senate Bill 53 (SB 53). “We support amending SB 53 to require frontier developers to maintain effective shutdown controls and an enforceable duty to use them when unsafe conditions arise, and no lesser intervention would adequately address the risk,” OpenAI wrote. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the two approaches address complementary needs. “The operator must contain the unsafe activity promptly. Independent review must examine both intervention and inaction,” he said. Newsom’s executive order , N-9-26, directs California’s Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and national experts, to submit recommendations by November 16 on potential amendments to existing AI safety laws. The order asks officials to examine independent verification inside AI laboratories, independent checks of safety assessments, verified shutdown mechanisms, and expanded reporting of critical safety incidents. It does not itself impose these proposed requirements. Independent verification Anthropic wants evaluators to assess developers’ safety claims and publish their own findings. “We strongly support requiring independent verification of what frontier AI companies report about the risks of their models and whether those risks are sufficiently mitigated,” the company wrote. It proposed requiring developers to publish risk reports at least every six months, covering serious risks from their models, including internally used models substantially riskier than released systems. Evaluators should receive unredacted reports and access to developers’ most capable models and relevant internal information. Anthropic also proposed that developers pay into a state-administered pooled fund to finance evaluators, rather than pay them directly. It said a team from the independent evaluation organization METR had received employee-like access on a pilot basis, with further partnerships involving SecureBio and Accenture under development. OpenAI, in its letter, said it supports independent technical assessments but distinguishes them from compliance audits. Technical assessments would examine evidence behind developers’ safety claims and the effectiveness of safeguards; compliance audits would check whether companies follow their published safety frameworks and legal obligations, it added. OpenAI recommended annual independent compliance audits and focused technical assessments of serious risks arising during model training, evaluation and internal deployment. It also urged California to work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop common assessment standards. Gogia said oversight requires more than funding. “Credible assurance must survive an adverse finding,” he said. articles.title: Teardown confirms Trump phone is a rebranded HTC U24 Pro
articles.content: JerryRigEverything has performed a teardown and durability test on the Trump phone This revealed that it's so similar to an HTC phone you can even swap their motherboards The Trump phone did at least survive the durability tests It was starting to feel like we wouldn’t have to hear any more about the Trump Mobile T1, but a new durability test has confirmed what we already largely knew — namely that it's little more than a rebranded HTC. A previous teardown from iFixit revealed that the Trump phone had essentially identical specs and components to the HTC U24 Pro — a mid-range Taiwanese phone from 2024. The design is ever so slightly different, with the Trump phone having a different camera housing and a gold paint job, but the dimensions are the same too. Now, though, JerryRigEverything has gone a step further, revealing that not only is the internal layout the same, right down to the number of screws, but if you swap the Trump phone’s motherboard with the HTC U24 Pro’s, both phones still work. So the Trump phone really is almost a carbon copy of that HTC handset — rather calling into question its claims of being “proudly American.” Passes the durability test The only upside to all this is that, by essentially being an HTC U24 Pro, the Trump phone matches that device for durability. It survived being bent in multiple directions, seemingly has effective water resistance, and has a screen that’s just as scratch-resistant as most modern smartphones. So if you have bought one of these devices, then at least it might last you a while — but that’s likely more down to designers and engineers in Taiwan than anyone in the US. And even if you haven’t bought one, the video is worth a watch, targeting as it does not just the phone but the entire Trump administration, to the point where one Reddit commenter described it as “the most entertaining durability test video I've ever seen”.

articles.title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time —Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability . ​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. Here’s what needs to change . Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century. Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming . —James Temple This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer. The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels. Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise . —Alexander C. Kaufman This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. articles.title: The five-star and TechRadar award-winning LG C6 OLED TV drops to a record-low price ahead of Black Friday — the ideal upgrade for GTA 6
articles.content: Are you waiting for Black Friday before picking up a brand new TV this year? Well, you might not need to, as this five-star-rated model — and our pick for the best TV you can buy this year in the TechRadar awards – is already down to a record-low price before the sales are even fully underway. Yep, the LG C6 65-inch OLED TV is now at Amazon for £1,699 (was £1,899). • See all LG OLED TV deals at Amazon If the 65-inch model is too large for your room or outside of your budget, several other sizes of this top-rated TV are also reduced to record-low prices right now. Amazon has the 42-inch LG C6 for £899 (was £999), the 48-inch LG C6 for £999 (was £1,099), and the 55-inch LG C6 for £1,199 (was £1,399). Whichever one you choose, you can be confident that you're getting the strongest all-around display for most people, according to our testing. The C6 is a top-tier OLED TV for streaming your favourite shows, watching 4K movies, enjoying fast-paced sports, or playing the latest games — especially something like GTA 6. One big question remains: will the price go lower as we get closer to Black Friday? Of course, we can never know for sure, but I would be surprised if the C6 gets any cheaper than this over the next few weeks. Maybe by a small amount of about £50 tops, but Black Friday deals usually stick around the same price for a longer time these days, so personally, I would be happy to buy now if you don't want to wait. LG C6 record-low price at Amazon C6 65-inch OLED TV: was £1899 now £1699 LG reclaimed the top spot on our best TV guide with the C6, as it boasts fantastic overall picture quality and excellent all-around performance, making it the number one pick for most. Contrast is top-tier, with vivid colours and rich blacks, while motion is handled expertly. No matter if you're watching films, streaming TV shows, playing games, or watching sports, it's up to the job. This is a record-low price for the top-tier TV and an early standout deal from this year's Black Friday sales. Smaller models from 42 inches also now start at £899. View Deal Want to read up more on this TV before hitting the buy button? Then you can check out our five-star review of the LG C6 . The brand has been leading the way in the world of OLED TVs for many years, and we concluded that this latest model is "a worthy successor to, and upgrade over, the LG C5." Our expert tester has praise for basically every part of the C6, saying that it offers fantastic picture quality, with superior brightness and excellent contrast, a modern processor to refine images, brilliant motion smoothing that makes fast-paced sports and games great to watch, and surprisingly strong built-in sound. It'll be worth investing in a soundbar eventually, though, for the best experience. The C6 is also one of the best options if you're hunting for a new gaming TV to prepare for GTA 6. It sports four HDMI 2.1 ports and a full suite of premium gaming features, such as support for 4K resolution at 165Hz, giving you a smooth and responsive experience when playing the latest games on current-gen consoles.

articles.title: Seattle-area startup Group14 raises $169M, plans battery materials factory in Spain
articles.content: Group14’s silicon anode facility began manufacturing materials in 2024. (Group14 Photo) Next-generation battery materials startup Group14 Technologies today announced $169 million in new funding and plans to build a manufacturing facility in Spain, expanding a production network that includes Washington state and South Korea. “In order to be a global player in a global industry, we need a global footprint, which means it’s not about picking one specific region and going all in,” Group14 CEO Rick Luebbe told GeekWire. “We really need to grow all regions.” The startup has developed a silicon-carbon material that replaces graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes, enabling higher energy density and faster charging, according to the company. The material already ships primarily to consumer-electronics customers, while the company pursues automotive and data center applications, Luebbe said. The funding came from a European investor, Luebbe said, but he did not name the firm. It extends the company’s $463 million Series D round and brings Group14’s total funding to nearly $1.5 billion. Rick Luebbe, CEO and co-founder of Group14. (GeekWire File Photo / Lisa Stiffler) The new facility will be located in Sagunto, near Valencia , with production targeted for mid-2029. Luebbe said the site offers clean energy, skilled labor from the chemical industry and proximity to automotive customers, given that Spain is the second-largest vehicle producer in Europe after Germany. Group14 already has a presence on the continent, acquiring Germany’s Schmid Silicon Technology Holding GmbH in 2023 to secure a European source of silane gas, a key ingredient in its battery material. Just as the U.S. has been working to bolster its domestic battery manufacturing and reduce its reliance on Chinese supplies, Europe is doing the same, Luebbe said. The company wants to be part of that solution and is eager to make its move. “Building chemical plants takes a long time, and so you’ve got to think ahead and be able to establish that global footprint and development strategy,” Luebbe said. “We’ve learned a lot in the lifetime of Group14.” Group14 was founded in 2015 and six years later began operating its first commercial-scale factory, called Battery Active Materials-1, or BAM-1, at its headquarters in Woodinville, Wash. In 2023, it broke ground on BAM-2 in central Washington’s Moses Lake with funding that included $100 million from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. The site has two modules that at full capacity will be able to produce up to 4,000 tons of silicon-carbon battery material annually, enough for at least 200,000 electric vehicles. The company originally aimed to start production by late 2024, a target later pushed to early 2026. Group14 laid off an undisclosed number of Washington workers in July 2025 and furloughed additional employees at Moses Lake in January as it shifted resources toward South Korea. Luebbe said this week that the company is now targeting mid-2027 to bring the first module online, following equipment installation and commissioning. The second module does not yet have a firm completion date. “It’s a very complicated infrastructure, and it takes a lot longer than we had anticipated to do the final installation and commissioning,” he added. Groups14’s battery materials facility in South Korea. (Group14 Photo) The company has at least secured the power it needs. It previously contracted sufficient clean energy to run the site, as well as a planned silane gas facility. Since Group14 began its development, data center deployments have accelerated in the region and projects are competing for clean electricity from hydropower dams. While BAM-2 has been delayed, Group14’s BAM-3 site in South Korea — which originally began as a joint venture with SK materials — has been producing anode material since 2024. articles.title: Attackers turn GitHub issues into supply chain campaign against 61 public repos in less than an hour
articles.content: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens. It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register . Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes. “Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register . Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised. "Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register . A novel attack chain They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy. First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point. “The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said. The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server. While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying. “The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said. Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.” Which repos were affected? As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects. The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular. Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K). “These projects are used by thousands…

articles.title: The 5 essential layers of AI agent sandboxing on Kubernetes
articles.content: An AI agent given autonomy to run code will inevitably run code no human has reviewed. It may install model-selected packages, run scripts generated moments earlier, and iterate until a developer’s test passes; that risk is limited to a laptop. For a company, it can extend beyond the agent’s workload to any workload deployed on shared Kubernetes infrastructure . Cluster configurations can limit a container’s system calls, but an allowed call that reaches a kernel vulnerability can still expose the underlying node. As agents proliferate, this gap has shifted workload isolation from a niche hardening requirement to a baseline need for platforms that run agents. This is a challenge our users at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) have asked us to help solve. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon takes place in Salt Lake City, Utah, from November 9 to 12. Register now. As expected in the cloud-native space, the community has developed solutions. These solutions exist across five layers: from the pod request, down to the node, and back up to the agent’s session. Platform teams can assemble the stack rather than reinvent it, while native provider support simplifies configuration and maintenance. Managed Kubernetes services offer sandboxed pods this way, but runtimes isolate agentic workloads differently . The following sections cover the options and tradeoffs before showing how the components fit together. Figure 1. The five layers of a pod sandboxing stack, each built from open-source components. 1. The isolation layer: choosing your risk boundary Figure 2. The same pod under three runtimes, with the boundary each one draws around agent code. First choose between minimal isolation, a restricted kernel interface, and full VM isolation. Each option comes with trade-offs between security and performance. runc offers the greatest performance through a shared host kernel. Seccomp-based filtering restricts the system calls a process can make. gVisor suits use cases where a restricted kernel interface is sufficient. Its user-space application kernel handles system calls instead of booting a guest Linux kernel, so the workload reaches the host through a small interface. gVisor implements a subset of Linux, so it starts quickly and packs densely. Applications must work with the interfaces Sentry implements, which can constrain agent behavior. “A separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents.” Kata Containers suit use cases requiring full VM isolation. Each pod runs in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel, at the cost of a VM boot and guest-kernel memory. Nearly anything that runs in a container runs in Kata. Agents exercise package managers, compilers, nested builds, and headless browsers. For that code, a separate guest kernel with hardware virtualization avoids surprises where system-call emulation falls short and unexpectedly handcuffs agents. 2. The node: assembling it and accounting for it Figure 3. Inside a worker node when a pod selects the Kata runtime. Everything outside the microVM runs on the host. Worker nodes must be configured for the selected sandboxed runtime. runc containers use Linux namespaces to separate process, filesystem, and network views, and cgroups to control resource use. They share the host kernel. Nodes need runc configured through a runtime such as containerd, but no guest kernel or hypervisor. gVisor handles workload system calls in Sentry, while a separate Gofer process mediates access to host-backed files. Each eligible node needs the gVisor runtime installed and integrated with containerd . Kata Containers place each pod in a lightweight VM. Workload system calls go to the guest Linux kernel, separated from the host by hardware-backed virtualization. This adds overhead and requires bare-metal nodes or VMs that support nested virtualization. In aKernel-based Virtual Machine ( KVM )…

articles.title: Why DoorDash is spending $17 billion to acquire Instacart
articles.content: DoorDash has agreed to acquire grocery rival Instacart for $17 billion, a deal that will bolster the delivery company’s move into grocery and boost business at the largest third-party delivery platform in America. Instacart, which launched in 2012, works with some 2,200 stores covering nearly 100,000 locations. DoorDash’s acquisition of the grocery delivery giant is a huge step toward its ultimate goal of revamping local business while owning all kinds of local delivery. DoorDash is still, fundamentally, a restaurant-delivery app. Delivery from restaurants in the U.S. remains the $73 billion company’s core business; in the second quarter of this year, restaurant order value grew as much as it did in all of 2022. In 2025, the company took in $13.7 billion in revenue (while it doesn’t break out revenue by category, it’s safe to assume most came from its restaurant business). But more and more DoorDash users are tapping the app for other purchases. In Q2 2026, members of the company’s DashPass subscription program placed roughly three-quarters of the company’s grocery and retail orders in the U.S. During an August earnings call, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu declared grocery the “fastest-growing part of our marketplace business.” DoorDash’s stock briefly dropped earlier this week on the news that it was pursuing an acquisition, a signal that at least some investors have concerns about the tie-in. The company has been on a spending spree lately. In the past 18 months, DoorDash dropped $3.9 billion on European delivery service Deliveroo, $1.2 billion on restaurant reservations platform SevenRooms, $300 million on Grubhub’s campus dining business, and a comparatively small $175 million on ad platform Symbiosys. The only category missing from this acquisition list: grocery. Unlocking grocery delivery DoorDash first added a handful of grocers to its app in the summer of 2020, when pandemic restrictions kept consumers home and the digital marketplace business boomed. A year later, DoorDash considered an Instacart acquisition, reportedly weighing a price of $40 billion to $50 billion for the online grocery delivery platform, which had also skyrocked in value during the pandemic. But the deal fell apart amid concerns about President Joe Biden’s antitrust enforcer Lina Khan, who was then-chair of the Federal Trade Commission. Instead, Instacart IPO’d in 2023, years past its pandemic peak, at a valuation of $10 billion. The timing may be better now. Retail giants Walmart and Amazon dominate online grocery, representing roughly half of its sales, leaving smaller retailers—including grocery chains like Albertsons, Fred Meyer, and Safeway—vying for the rest. Those retailers partner with companies like Instacart for delivery. Earlier this year, market research firm eMarketer estimated Instacart will control roughly 65% of the third-party U.S. grocery delivery market in 2026. That market share alone might be enough to pique DoorDash’s interest, but Instacart is actually complementary to DoorDash in several ways. It’s the largest third-party grocery delivery platform by sales—in Q2 2026, Instacart sold $10.35 billion worth of goods through its network—and DoorDash claims it leads in retail order volume. (The company doesn’t break down its sales by vertical, but recently said it expected its grocery and retail unit economics to turn positive in the second half of the year.) Both companies are working on tech solutions for in-store inventory management and data collection. In September, Instacart announced a new initiative to map, in real time, store shelves, giving in-store managers a virtual, aisle-by-aisle view of their products. Days later, DoorDash launched a similar offering, marketed to consumer packaged goods brands, that uses couriers to photograph shelves while picking items for customers, mapping availability and sharing more data, like which items customers are likely to substitute when something is missing. Together, these tools would…

articles.title: Score a huge $1,250 saving on this Alienware gaming PC with an RTX 5070 Ti and 32GB DDR5 right now
articles.content: You don't have to settle for huge price rises in the PC hardware market. Thanks to Newegg, there's a $1,250 discount right now on a 4K-capable Alienware Aurora DACT1250 gaming PC with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti and 32GB of DDR5 RAM for $2,599.99 . ● Check out this deal at Newegg This is Dell's premium brand for gamers and, as you can expect from a premium brand, the prices are usually towards the top end. The $1,250 discount here means you'll be saving a huge sum on a gaming PC with serious firepower for 4K gameplay, putting it at a much better price than you would get elsewhere. This DACT1250 model also comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 285 CPU and a 1TB SSD for storage. Aurora DACT1250: was $3849.99 now $2599.99 This Alienware Aurora gaming PC is a powerhouse for 4K gaming. It features an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU, a 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 285 CPU, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD. View Deal Front and center here is the Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti . This is one of Nvidia's newest Blackwell GPUs but, more importantly, it's the third most powerful consumer GPU of Nvidia's current-gen lineup. It has 8,960 CUDA cores and 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM, operating on a bigger 256-bit memory bus. This is a card that'll smash through 1080p with the highest frame rates, taking you up to 1440p and 4K with ease. The VRAM boost to 16GB is important because it means your PC has the opportunity to switch up to 1440p or 4K and run games at high and even graphic presets at those resolutions. 4K, especially with ray tracing switched on, might require a few tweaks to your settings, or involve you falling back on Nvidia DLSS with multi-frame generation for an AI-helped uplift, adding extra frames into the mix for smoother gameplay. The Bench charts and our GPU benchmarks place the RTX 5070 Ti pretty highly compared to rival GPUs. For the CPU, you're getting the Intel Core Ultra 9 285 here. It ships with 24 cores, eight of which are performance cores, which'll be good for high-performance gaming. You also get 16 efficient cores for multi-threaded tasks. Unlike the 285K, the 285 is locked, meaning you can't overclock it. You get clock speeds as high as 5.7 GHz with the performance cores in action here, though. This Arrow Lake CPU hasn't been a big hitter in the gaming world, admittedly, but the raw power of the RTX 5070 Ti is still formidable, and should help to compensate. Elsewhere, though, you're getting 32GB of DDR5 memory, so you won't see a bottleneck as far as system RAM is concerned. There's also a 1TB SSD included here, giving you space for a few big games alongside a Windows installation on the same drive. The $1,250 saving on this pre-built Alienware Aurora DACT1250 gaming PC is a serious bargain, and it means you'll only pay $2,599.99 compared to the original $3,849.99 list price. The RTX 5070 Ti in this build means you've got a GPU ready for 4K gaming, with specs that should keep you going for years to come.

articles.title: Garmin Messenger is placing too much trust in SMS verification, and this might not end well
articles.content: TL;DR A Garmin Messenger user reports restoring their entire chat history on a second phone using only SMS verification, without a Garmin account password. The findings raise concerns that recycled phone numbers could let new owners access previous conversations, including sensitive location information. Garmin has reportedly been informed of the issue, but it hasn’t confirmed a fix. Handing over an old phone number shouldn’t mean handing over your private conversations. But a Garmin Messenger user has raised an uncomfortable question: Could the next person assigned your number inherit your chats, too? In a Reddit post , the user describes installing Garmin Messenger on a second, freshly set-up phone. They entered their existing number, verified an SMS code, and watched their previous conversations reappear. No Garmin account password was required. The second phone reportedly also began sending and receiving messages, with no obvious way to view or remotely disconnect other sessions.
articles.author: Hillary Keverenge

articles.title: Russia orders Apple to surrender users' messages on demand
articles.content: Apple and Microsoft have been added to a Russian state surveillance registry, requiring them to hand over users' text, video and audio messages without a legal process, and by request. Moscow at night (Credit: Evgenit/Pixabay) Multiple firms and apps are already on this same list, including WhatsApp and Telegram, so it's not clear why it has taken until now for Apple to be added. It's a continuation of the country's moves to control users' messages, though, as it follows Russia's blocking of FaceTime in 2025. According to Bloomberg , Apple and Microsoft were added to this registry of "organizers of information dissemination" on October 2, 2026. The registry is operated by the country's state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, which previously forced Apple to remove VPN apps from the App Store . Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Which laptop should you buy?
articles.content: Apple has just announced two new flagship laptops: the MacBook Pro OLED and the MacBook Pro M6 . The former is the company’s first touchscreen OLED MacBook, while the latter updates last year’s MacBook Pro M5 . Both should be fantastic laptops for pro users, but which one should you buy? We haven't tested either of these new MacBooks yet, but based on what we know, they shouldn’t have trouble landing on our best MacBooks page. To that end, here’s everything you need to know about the MacBook Pro OLED and MacBook Pro M6 to help you decide which one is right for you. Also, be sure to read our hands-on with the MacBook Pro OLED from the Apple "Pro and Tell" event ! MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Specs MacBook Pro M6 (starting) MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (starting) Price $1,999 $2,899 Display 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR (3024x1964 pixels), 120Hz 14.2-inch PROLED XDR (3024 x 1986 pixels), 120Hz, multi-touch Display finish Standard glass, nano-texture glass Standard glass, nano-texture glass Colors Silver, Space Black Silver, Space Black Chip M6 (12-core CPU, 12-core GPU) M5 Pro (18-core CPU, 20-core GPU) Memory 16GB 24GB Storage 1TB 1TB Ports 3 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3 3 x Thunderbolt 5, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack, 1 x SD card reader, 1 x MagSafe 3 OS macOS 27 Golden Gate macOS 27 Golden Gate Connectivity Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread (Apple N1) Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread (Apple N1) Camera 12MP Center Stage webcam 12MP Center Stage webcam Size 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches 14 x 9.62 x 0.63 inches Weight 3.4 pounds 4 pounds MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Price (Image credit: Apple edited with Gemini) There’s no denying that both new MacBook models cost a pretty penny. That said, one is definitely more affordable than the other (relatively speaking). The 14-inch MacBook Pro OLED with the M5 Pro chip, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch model with the same specs starts at $3,399. If you want a laptop with the M5 Max chip, the 14-inch model starts at $4,499, while the 16-inch model is $4,799. Then we have the 14-inch MacBook Pro, which starts at $1,999 and packs an M6 chip with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage. You can add up to 32GB of RAM and 4TB of storage, though that’ll substantially bring up the price. MacBook Pro OLED vs MacBook Pro M6: Display (Image credit: Future) The biggest difference between these two MacBooks is their respective displays. The MacBook Pro OLED is the first MacBook with a touchscreen OLED panel, while the MacBook Pro M6 keeps the mini-LED screen of current MacBooks. Depending on what you want or need, this could be the main determining factor in which MacBook you’d buy. According to Apple, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display “offers a visual experience unlike any other." That’s no doubt because of the tandem OLED panel, which promises true per-pixel blacks and zero blooming around UI elements. Apple claims this display can deliver peak SDR and HDR brightness of 2000 nits, which is absolutely eye-scorching. Apple says the tandem OLED technology keeps brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display. The company also says it precisely calibrates each display for consistency. On top of that—and I mean that literally—the notch cutout at the top of the panel has been replaced by the Dynamic Island you’ve seen on the best iPhones . This brings Live Activities to the MacBook for the first time. Lastly, the MacBook Pro OLED has a touchscreen. Apple says it crafted touch input specifically for the Mac, with a touch sensor built directly into the display panel, not layered on top. Our own Mark Spoonauer went hands-on with the MacBook Pro OLED and said that the touchscreen support feels “pretty smooth” as he navigated between apps or used his finger to draw. However, it doesn’t support the Apple Pencil. Display benchmarks MacBook Pro M5 MacBook Pro M4 Nits…

articles.title: LibreOffice's 'no AI' stance meets LLM-assisted code
articles.content: The Document Foundation (TDF) says LibreOffice has no built-in AI features and that its core developers do not use LLMs - but community contributors face different rules. In a Fediverse post , someone who goes by the handle of argv[-1] highlights three LibreOffice commits this year that acknowledge the use of LLM coding assistants. Two of them – Inheritance when setting paragraph style font size to 100% or +0pt and Enable relative font sizes in Calc cell styles – date from April and credit Claude with helping identify the fixes. More recently, September's Add Copy Image button to screenshot dialog acknowledges using GitHub Copilot in VS Code to generate the BitmapTransferable class, while the copyButtonHandler method was written manually with LLM/code-completion assistance. This is hardly a fatal flaw – after all, it's getting hard to find any major FOSS project with absolutely no LLM-generated code in it these days. However, The Document Foundation says that the leading FOSS office suite is AI-free. As we noted when it released version 26.8 in August , we interpret this statement as a jab at its former development partner Collabora. Back in June, we noted that increased AI integration was a headline feature in Collabora CODE 26.04 . CODE is Collabora's web-based office suite, based on LibreOffice code. TDF – the primary maintainer and custodian of LibreOffice since its 2010 fork from Oracle-controlled OpenOffice.org – has made the absence of built-in AI a selling point. In September, it published a blog post declaring that no AI is now a feature . Meanwhile, on October 21, TDF announced 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks – excluding Windows updates and downloads of older releases, which are counted separately. The foundation acknowledged that the reasons for the growth are difficult to determine. TDF's direct response on Mastodon is dismissive: "Ah, another high-quality Mastodon discussion. Again: No core developers use LLMs. We rely on contributions from the wider community and don't explicitly list tools people can't use – but we do require people disclose when they use LLMs and generally discourage the practice. We carefully review submissions by contributors to make sure the code quality is good and that the patch author understands their own code. LLMs are prohibited for students. That is not 'slop'." In other words, TDF's approach resembles what some commenters have compared to the Debian approach : LLM coding assistants are permitted for some contributors, subject to disclosure and human review. For AI advocates, this is the only pragmatic response – which could be summarized as the "AI is just a tool" school of thought. However, since this admission does seem to contradict the very visible public no-AI message, some LibreOffice users are really rather unhappy. Our favorite comment so far is from Argentinian developer Federico Schonborn , who slyly noted : "When a bakery announces they won't put asbestos in their cake frosting you must not point out they're already putting asbestos in their cake filling, you see." We asked TDF’s spokesman Italo Vignoli for comment. He pointed us to TDF's Development/AI policy , and added: "There isn't any departure from the public statements about LO 26.8, as they were about user features and not about development." As "Skjeggtroll" succinctly put it : "It strikes me as odd to ban all use of LLM for the commit message , but still allow its use for the actual code." ®

articles.title: This beefy Android handheld quietly got a gigantic, 10,000mAh battery
articles.content: Credit: MANGMI TL;DR The MANGMI Pocket Max has quietly received a battery capacity upgrade, going from 8,000mAh to 10,000mAh. This means it might have the largest battery out of any Android handheld on the market. The handheld otherwise offers a Snapdragon 865 chip, a 7-inch 144Hz OLED screen, and a base 8GB/128GB model for $230. The MANGMI Pocket Max is one of the most notable large Android handhelds on the market, delivering a 7-inch 144Hz OLED screen and an 8,000mAh battery for ~$230. That battery is pretty competitive for a large handheld, but it turns out that the company stealthily upgraded the capacity. The Pocket Max product page reveals that the device now comes with a 10,000mAh battery instead of the existing 8,000mAh pack (spotted via r/sbcgaming ). It’s unclear when this change took place, but it was still listed with an 8,000mAh battery in the most recently archived product page (August 6).
articles.author: Hadlee Simons
