articles.title: Forget iPhone Duo, this iPhone is lighter, more durable and $100 off
articles.content: The iPhone Duo is very hard to come by, even with the problems some early adopters have been having with the screen. It's worth remembering that it's not the only special edition iPhone on sale right now, and if you want something cheaper and more durable, you can pick one up for $100 off the normal price. I am, of course, talking about the iPhone Air, which is now $999 at Best Buy. That's $100 off the normal price, and you can pick up the phone delivered tomorrow -- assuming you don't want a same-day store pickup. The iPhone Air may be a year old at this point, but it's still a great phone with a lot of great qualities. The iPhone Air suffered a price hike earlier this year, but Best Buy has brought it back to the original $999 price tag. This phone is slim, durable, and extremely lightweight -- complete with all the same benefits as other iPhones. Plus it's a lot easier to get hold of than the iPhone Duo. View Deal The iPhone Air's main selling point is that it's incredibly light and thin. It's not quite as thin as the iPhone Duo , which is 0.20-inches thin compared to the iPhone Air's 0.22-inches. However it is a heck of a lot lighter than the 8.96 ounce iPhone Duo, with a total weight of just 5.82 ounces. That should make it a lot more comfortable to use and carry around. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The Air also packs in a 6.5-inch display, complete with the same 1-120Hz adaptive refresh rate you'd get on a standard iPhone, and our tests recorded a maximum brightness of 1,678 nits. Performance is offered by the A19 chip which, while not as impressive as the A20 Pro, is still one of the best mobile chipsets around at the moment. The camera performance is pretty good, though it is hampered by the fact there's only a single main camera. The lack of ultrawide and telephoto lenses is obvious, and that's the trade-off for purchasing a super-skinny phone like this. One of the best things about the iPhone Air is its durability, though. It has all the standard iPhone protections, including Ceramic Shield 2 display glass alongside IP68 water and dust resistance. It also comes with a titanium build, one of only two iPhones to offer the super-strong metal, and is surprisingly resistant to being bent. Which was a real concern before this phone was announced. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The iPhone Air gets all the benefits of iOS 27 , including the full suit of Apple Intelligence features. That's right, it has the 12GB of RAM needed to run on-device features like Siri Expressive Voices and enhanced dictation. However it does lack features like stylus support, multitasking and the faster charging speed you'll get on more advanced iPhones. The battery life also isn't as good, roughly 12 hours in our testing, on account of the skinny design. Still if you want a stylish iPhone that's sure to turn some heads, be sure to pick up the iPhone Air. Because you'll actually get hold of one before the holidays.
articles.author: Tom Pritchard

articles.title: Want to keep a cool head? Get a pair of top-rated cooling pillows with 10% off at Casper
articles.content: If you're regularly waking up with a sore neck then it's time to think about upgrading to a better pillow. And if you spent the summer fruitlessly searching for the cold side, I've found the perfect deal for you: a pair of Casper Hybrid Snow Pillows for $322.20, down from $358 . I know what you're thinking. Over $300 for a pair of pillows? Are they some kind of magic pillows with supernatural cooling powers? And honestly, the answer's yes. They're our top-rated cooling pick in our best pillows guide. And not only do they keep temperatures down at night, they're also incredibly comfortable in just about every sleeping position. With the Black Friday mattress sales coming soon we're bound to see some great deals on all kinds of pillows. But if you want the best cooling option I don't think this deal is likely to be bettered. Here's what you need to know: Hybrid Snow Pillow Double Pack (standard): was $358 now $322.20 The Casper Hybrid Snow Pillow features some seriously impressive cooling technology: a cooling cover, phase change material and Casper's own HeatDelete bands, plus a combination of ultra-soft foam and down-alternative fiber that make this pillow both supportive and breathable. There's 10% off when you buy a double pack, bringing two standard size pillows down to $322.20, while a king size pair will cost you $376.20 (down from $418). Our Casper Hybrid Snow Pillow review : ★★★★½ User score : ★★★½ (380+ reviews) View Deal What's so special about the Casper Snow Hybrid Pillow? This isn't a cheap pillow, but in our Casper Hybrid Snow Pillow review our tester absolutely raved about its cooling prowess as well as the comfort and support it offered. She found that the pillow was cool to the touch, and that its combination of AirScape foam and HeatDelete bands enabled heat to escape rather than building up during the night. It earned 5.5 out of 5 stars for cooling — a rating not seen before or since. (Image credit: Future) She was also impressed that despite being less lofty than other pillows she's tested, the Casper Hybrid Snow Pillow delivered a near-perfect mix of luxurious comfort and squishy support. In short, she described it as one of the best pillows she's ever tested. That said, though, if the price is still a little high for you and you're not sure you really need all that cooling technology, there's another option that'll give you all that dreamy comfort and support for less money... Hybrid Pillow Double Pack (standard): was $258 now $232.20 Don't need high-end cooling technology in your pillow? The Casper Hybrid Pillow offers all the comfort and support of the Hybrid Snow without the cooling tech, at a more affordable price point. The same 10% off deal for a double pack is available right now, and a pair of standard pillow will cost you $232.20, while a king size pack is down to $286.20 from $318. It's still a premium buy, but your head and neck will love you for it. User score : ★★★★ (490+ reviews) View Deal

articles.title: I hope the Motorola Signature 27 is great, but I have 2 big concerns I can’t shake
articles.content: Credit: Motorola Maybe I just like rooting for the underdog, but I can’t help but feel that the US smartphone market could do with a good shake-up. Loosening the grip of Apple, Google, and Samsung would inject a little more urgency into the pace of hardware innovation. While phones like the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max and vivo X500 Pro Max offer global consumers something different, they’re not available in the US. At least not without the inconvenience and expense of importing a unit. Thankfully, Motorola remains a major player stateside, and the upcoming Signature 27 is officially heading to the US for the lineup’s second generation.

articles.title: Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done
articles.content: More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots. Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1 , the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low. Smaller Series B rounds grow scarcer One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds. So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data. The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set. Big rounds still a big thing On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular. At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals. Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus , Jeff Bezos ’ physical AI startup that launched last year. Model developer World Labs , led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li , was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor. For a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients. Mostly an AI story Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group. So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories. AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies. Bullish climate for Series B Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed. Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies. articles.title: Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups
articles.content: Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning. U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done. Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase . Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020. Size your seed against the Series A Uncork Capital ‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal. A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic , a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed , right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures , then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later. Map your Series A leads now Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything. Sell your way to the bar The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion. At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine. From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside. A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one. As the co-founder and managing partner of MGV , Marc Schröder is committed to establishing MGV as the premier venture firm for world-class tech entrepreneurs to accelerate their visions. Under Schröder’s stewardship, MGV has swiftly ascended to a top-quartile firm, surpassing the performance of 95% of venture funds. Business Insider has recognized him as one of the Top 100 global seed investors , and his perspectives are published regularly in Crunchbase News and other leading publications. articles.title: SpaceX no longer needs NASA, and that's a problem for America's space agency
articles.content: For nearly a quarter of a century, Elon Musk and his essential partner at SpaceX, Gwynne Shotwell, viewed the United States government as El Dorado, the mythical city of gold. Like machete-wielding treasure hunters, Musk and Shotwell hacked through a tangled jungle filled with lurking carnivores such as Boeing and Lockheed Martin, as well as bean counters and regulators. Over time, against long odds, the pair cleared a path for SpaceX to contracts at NASA and the US military. They sued when things did not go their way. They hollered about unfair playing fields. Most importantly, they delivered quality space products to the US government for less. And so, after a while, SpaceX found El Dorado and a city of contracts. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Traces of new Pi hardware spotted in GitHub
articles.content: The wait for a new Raspberry Pi Zero may be nearly over, judging by the raspberrypi/linux repository. Among the merged pull requests is one titled "Add device tree for Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4A," suggesting new hardware is on the way, including a successor to the very long-in-the-tooth Pi Zero 2 W. The board launched five years ago. Its 512 MB of memory was hardly generous, but it offered considerable bang for the buck. At the time, we reckoned performance was closer to the Raspberry Pi 3 than the flagship Pi 4, but perfectly adequate provided you didn't open too many browser tabs at once. According to the source tree, as reported by Phoronix , the new board could use the Broadcom BCM271, up from the RP3A0 in the current Zero. If so, that would be a significant performance gain, though it's unclear whether the 1.5GHz clock speed of the Pi 4, which uses the same SoC, will be retained. Heat is a concern as the Pi 4 gained a reputation for running hot under load without active cooling, and it throttles performance when temperatures climb. A board as small as the Zero will have even less room to shed heat. Assuming that challenge can be met, it would be a worthy upgrade for the venerable Pi Zero 2. There is no word on how much memory it is likely to have – we can't imagine much given the current cost of RAM and the need to keep the price at least close to that of the Zero 2 W, which can still be had for around $18. The code also hints at eMMC storage is mentioned, but that seems unlikely to reach the finished product, probably because of the cost. Alongside the Pi Zero 3 W is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. Where the Zero 3 W is a clear upgrade, the 4 Model A looks more like a cost-cutting measure amid rising hardware prices. Model A boards typically have less memory, and no Ethernet port, and the 4A appears to have a single HDMI output rather than twp. Things could change before any hardware ships. We asked Raspberry Pi if anything was in the pipeline, but the company said it had nothing to add. Enthusiasts will welcome an upgraded Pi Zero after more than half a decade, provided the price is right and it doesn't run too hot. At the same time, a cut-down Pi 4 carries the whiff of inevitability in an era of rising component costs. ®

articles.title: “Urgency is an inherently subjective call”: Anthropic tells TNS how it grades Claude Duet
articles.content: Anthropic built Claude Duet , an AI assistant that monitors your connected apps and works on tasks in the background, to decide what needs your attention without being asked. A week after its October 21 debut, the frontier lab with an IPO in its sights has shared with The New Stack how it is testing whether Duet gets those priorities right. Anthropic has developed internal graders to assess how Duet prioritizes tasks, though urgency can be subjective. The stakes rise when an agent manages work across email, calendars, and B2B apps. Duet can remain within its permissions and still get its priorities wrong. Powered by Claude Opus 5.5 , Duet can prepare work and flag items it thinks need attention without waiting for instructions. Anthropic has been testing that approach with its own employees, using their day-to-day work to see how Duet handles competing priorities. Testing Duet’s judgment “After using Duet for our day-to-day work at Anthropic, we calibrated graders that assess correctness in task prioritization, and we run them offline against cases representative of internal use and early external testing,” a company representative tells The New Stack . Those graders measure whether Duet can distinguish what deserves attention from what can wait, though Anthropic acknowledges the difficulty of evaluating those decisions. “Urgency is an inherently subjective call, so we found building an eval for it imperfect but quite helpful,” a company representative says. Duet can spot tasks like an approaching deadline or an email requiring a reply, but it doesn’t always know which task should be a priority, and the company admits the agent can misread conversations or misjudge urgency. Anthropic’s public launch and support materials do not say how often that happens. Testing Duet’s safeguards On October 23, two days after Duet’s debut, Anthropic published a closer look at its safety, privacy, and security safeguards . Duet team lead Karan Ahuja pointed to the post while addressing feedback received through messages, emails, and public posts. We’ve been humbled by the interest in Claude Duet, and are working hard to get people off the waitlist. In the meantime, a few thoughts based on DMs, emails, posts we’ve seen. → Who can use it: Pro and Max subscribers in the US, for now. → Where: You can use it on iOS,… pic.twitter.com/9MMMZbHpLw — karan ahuja (@ahuja_karan) October 23, 2026 Anthropic keeps the part of Duet that does the work separate from the part that checks whether the work matches what the user actually asked for. “A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on the auto mode classifier from Claude Code and extended for Claude Duet,” the rep tells The New Stack . “It assesses whether the action matches your intent.” Because that check runs independently of the model performing the task, Anthropic says instructions hidden in a webpage can’t directly steer the classifier’s decision. Anthropic says an outside firm penetration-tested Duet, but its public materials don’t show how reliably the separate check catches actions outside the user’s intent. Related research illustrates the difficulty of enforcing this agent scope: Researchers found that removing a prompt section defining authorized and out-of-scope actions in Claude Code tests increased out-of-scope actions, although that study did not test Duet’s separate classifier. Limiting prompt injection The separation is designed to reduce prompt injection, where malicious instructions embedded in emails, documents, or webpages try to redirect an agent. Researchers have already explored this risk by leaving hidden messages for rogue agents and observing how they responded. Anthropic’s support materials still tell users to review drafts and approval requests because Duet may encounter prompt injection. Duet uses the apps…

articles.title: Google Struggling to Make AI Mode Searches Pay
articles.content: Alphabet shares fell nearly 10% after Google disclosed that searches through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The Register reports: Alphabet on Wednesday reported its Q3 results, which included news that its year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years. Some of that growth comes from users adopting "AI Mode" -- Google's latest LLM-powered search system. Google's revenue from search rose 12 percent year-over-year to $63.25 billion, a little lower than the 14.5 percent growth the company reported in last year's Q3. During Alphabet's earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the slowdown was caused by "lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." That's a worry given that Google is spending enormous sums on infrastructure. $51.4 billion went out the door in Q3, around two thirds of it going towards servers and networking equipment. The rest funded datacenter builds. That spending appears to have impacted profitability, as Alphabet reported $26.17 billion net income for the quarter. Last year's Q3, during which Google revenue was $102.35 billion, produced $35 billion net income. Schindler argued that AI search will pay off. "On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent," he told investors. "In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time." Google tried to seize one of those opportunities today, by turning on ads alongside AI Mode searches around the world, after first testing them in the US only. But for now, AI Mode searches aren't as lucrative as Google's existing search business, which brought in just under half of Alphabet's $125.8 billion quarterly revenue. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The iPhone 18 Pro is the antithesis to Android’s AI era
articles.content: I don’t need to reiterate that the tech industry has spent the past couple of years trying to convince us that AI is the next step of computing and that it needs to be shoehorned into every computing touchpoint. And as far as smartphones go, Android is at the forefront of this push. For better or worse, Google has integrated Gemini into every aspect of the Android experience, be it messaging or photography, search and more. The end goal is pretty obvious – your phone should know what you need, anticipate your next move, and help you get things done without having to ask. Basically, an agentic future.

articles.title: Apple Announced Scott Forstall's Departure 14 Years Ago Today
articles.content: Fourteen years ago today, Apple announced that iOS chief Scott Forstall would leave the company the following year, serving as an advisor to Tim Cook in the interim. Reports at the time said Forstall refused to sign Apple's public apology for the poor coverage of Apple Maps, dismissing the problems as exaggerated, leaving Cook's name on the letter instead. Forstall kept a low profile until 2015, when he resurfaced as a Broadway producer , winning a Tony for Fun Home . Elsewhere this month, Apple's Polishing Cloth turned five . articles.title: Microsoft breaks New Outlook attachment opening with Edge Update
articles.content: Users of New Outlook wondering where the option to open an attachment went have a culprit to blame – an Edge update. The issue underscores how interconnected things are in the Microsoft ecosystem. According to the vendor, an update to Edge 156 "unintentionally enabled an unnecessary configuration," which means some New Outlook users are unable to open email file attachments. An error stating the file cannot be opened also appears for some, along with an instruction to restart Outlook. However, the "Open" option goes away after the error is encountered. A workaround is to use "Save As" to save the attachment, and then open the file manually. Microsoft confirmed the issue yesterday afternoon in the advisory EX1528992, and early this morning began rolling out a fix to disable the "unnecessary" configuration. It expects that it'll take 12 hours for the fix to be rolled out, and users will have to close and reopen New Outlook to feel the benefit. The problem raises some interesting questions. While we'd understand how something unexpected in Edge might cause rendering issues in New Outlook, losing the ability to open attachments because of something an Edge update did is concerning and may make some administrators reconsider the blast radius of software updates. We asked Microsoft for more information about the "unnecessary configuration" and will update this piece should it respond. However, the incident highlights connections within Windows that might surprise users. In addition, it shows that, despite a woeful showing on the desktop market share front – although Edge recently "surged" to almost 15 percent last month, according to Statcounter, up from around 10 percent for much of the year – Microsoft's browser can still capture user attention. It's just not the sort of attention the Windows maker might have hoped for. It is also worth noting that Outlook Classic does not appear to be affected by the issue (according to Microsoft's EX1528992 advisory for Exchange Online). Impacted users could therefore temporarily add opening attachments to the list of things the old software does that the new software doesn't. ®

articles.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.content: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely. Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important. With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken. Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved…
articles.author: Madhulika Srikumar, Claire Leibowicz

articles.title: I’ve tested plenty of chargers, but this is the one staying on my desk
articles.content: A charger is one of those accessories we use every single day but rarely think much about. If there’s one thing I’ve learned from testing and spending money on quite a few chargers over the past few months, it’s that investing in a good one can make your life a lot easier. I’ve tried everything from compact chargers that take up almost no space to more powerful ones designed to charge multiple devices. But throughout my testing, I looked for something specific: a charger that could power my laptop and phone at the same time, charge both devices fast, and save me the hassle of reaching for two different adapters. After all, why carry multiple chargers when one can do the job? I’ve come across plenty of options that work well, but one charger in particular caught my attention. I liked it so much that I’ve decided to keep using it.

articles.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
articles.content: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century. A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries. A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds. Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group. At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds. But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue. So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story ). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands…

articles.title: Our world runs on satellites. What happens when we can’t launch more?
articles.content: “Like riding a broomstick in a hurricane.” This is reportedly how one SpaceX engineer described the intense atmospheric reentry of the first Falcon 9 rocket to go to space and then successfully land back here. That moment, on December 21, 2015, marked the beginning of a dizzying decade-long spell for the space sector, as engineers no longer had to worry about getting their technology into space. Now, the industry’s main challenges were building enough satellites, raising enough capital, finding enough customers. It’s important to remember how fundamental space is to ordinary life. It’s no exaggeration to call it the backbone of the world economy. Satellites tell ships, aircraft, cars, and phones where they are; keep large parts of the financial system and communications networks on time; carry data across oceans and remote areas; forecast the weather; and watch crops, roads, fires, floods, and supply chains. And that’s to say nothing of defense. Satellites let armed forces communicate, navigate, track threats, guide weapons, and see what’s happening far beyond what they can see. With Falcon 9, SpaceX slashed the cost of reaching orbit. It increased the frequency of launch and, through reusability, it transformed launch from an infrequent, bespoke event into something closer to normal. The satellite operator SES, where I spent three decades, including as CTO, had been SpaceX’s first commercial customer to launch a satellite to geostationary transfer orbit in 2013. We became the first commercial customer to fly on a reused Falcon 9 booster. A new landscape But things change. And SpaceX is now moving into its Starship era. Falcon 9, expected to keep flying until around 2030, is no longer taking reservations. The main manufacturing and engineering center for the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in Hawthorne, California, is being wound down, and SpaceX is redirecting people and resources to Louisiana, where its $100 billion spaceport is being built. In September, Starship reached orbit for the first time, despite an engine failure, and deployed a fleet of Starlink satellites. If it works as intended, its capacity will dwarf Falcon 9’s. But commercial satellite operators shouldn’t assume that all this capacity will be theirs to buy. First of all, SpaceX has its own voracious appetite for launch. Starlink is the world’s largest satellite constellation by far, and the new V3 satellites, deployed by Starship, are crucial to its expansion. NASA depends on Starship for its lunar ambitions, while demand for SpaceX from the U.S. Department of Defense keeps growing. Starship may create vast capacity but with it may come vast internal and government demand for it. The next frontier What, then, for the commercial companies? There is no simple answer. Yes, there are alternative companies, and they are getting better and better, but they are years behind SpaceX. Europe’s Ariane 6 is flying regularly, but not operating at anything like the rate of Falcon 9. New Glenn and Vulcan are important additions to the market, as is Neutron. Relativity Space’s Terran R is also promising, though it remains a few years from commercial service. None, however, combine the frequency, reliability, and cost of launch that Falcon 9 achieved. Amazon Leo, a nascent satellite constellation-based internet provider, has booked more than 100 launches across several space companies, including Ariane 6, recently increasing its order from 18 to 24 missions. Defense customers want larger, more widely distributed constellations. There’s no doubt that if the launch bottleneck I’ve described isn’t addressed, the price of launch will increase significantly. But cost may ultimately matter less than availability. This will undoubtedly change the nature of competition in the space sector. The companies with the strongest balance sheets will be able to book launches years in advance, diversify across providers, and potentially absorb the cost…

articles.title: Matrix takes sovereign messaging into the realm of the tech giants
articles.content: Decentralized messaging platform Matrix is no longer the upstart it once was. The organization is now a serious challenger to the status quo as concerns about sovereignty and independence reach new heights. At the organization's recent Malmo event, which grew attendance 30 percent year-on-year, the mood shifted from "yes, this is important" to "yes, we're rolling this out." Matrix is an open standard for communication. It's a federated system, so there are no central hubs or overseas control to worry about, and it can be used for anything from messaging to voice over IP. Video is also supported. The system is an alternative to services such as Microsoft Teams. It has become popular in the public sector as governments grow increasingly wary of relying on US tech giants for services that the Trump administration could switch off at will . However, that increased interest and subsequent roll-outs have brought a level of scrutiny Matrix was not fully prepared for. A recent report regarding anonymous reaction to a roll-out of the technology by the European Commission took Element - the company that puts the lion share of the money into Matrix - by surprise. One attendee at the Malmo conference observed, "First they [competitors] ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you." Matrix remains an open standard, however, the open source foundation behind it would certainly welcome more paying members. "It's true that we're definitely getting more attention than we have had before," said Element CEO Matthew Hodgson. "We are seeing Matrix ending up on the critical path of digital sovereignty as almost the poster child of the whole thing. "I'm not sure that we necessarily do want to be the poster child," he added, "We didn't sign up to end up being ambassadors for digital sovereignty, roaming from government to government, but empirically that's where we've ended up, and yeah, that's going to attract attention from people who would rather everyone just kept in their traditional big tech systems." This comes amid worries about the reliability of international partners, from early projects including France's Tchap messenger for the public sector and Germany's BundesMessenger through to more recent users, such as the Swedish public sector. Indeed, in one memorable demonstration during the Matrix event, messages were sent between French, Swedish, and NATO entities. "I cannot overstate the strangeness," Hodgson added, "of having various national militaries phoning up every couple of days, saying, 'Look, we need to get on board Matrix too because we need to talk to this country and they're using Matrix, and we need to talk to that country, and they're using Matrix.'" "It could be for defense, could be national security, could just be healthcare or education, public sector. But that is real. That is why there is a feeding frenzy." Not that Element or Matrix is trying to build a better Teams than Teams. Patrick Alberts, Element's Chief Product Officer, said, "This is a digitally sovereign communication solution that, by and large, works like Teams in many aspects, but it's not set out to be the faster Porsche here..." As for the reported complaints from the European Commission over Element's software implementation, Diana Gheorghe, EC head of sector for Communication and Collaboration Services, addressed them directly and described the anonymous complaints as "the natural friction of [a] high-profile rollout that we have done at scale." Alexandru Vignide, EC service manager for Communication and Collaboration Services, who is very much at the pointy end of making the sovereign communication tools work, noted the speed of the rollout, which began with a proof of concept in Q4 2025, and hit laptops between July and September 2026. The EC chose the Schengen Cloud Alliance (which includes OVHcloud) for hosting and, according to Vignide, "We wanted to provide a familiar experience for users." Not everyone is impressed with what is rolling…

articles.title: Trump Phone passes the bend test, fails the originality test
articles.content: TL;DR JerryRigEverything puts the Trump Mobile T1 through scratch, bend, and teardown tests, with the phone surviving the physical punishment. The teardown reveals internals identical to the two-year-old HTC U24 Pro, reinforcing earlier findings from an iFixit investigation. Swapping the motherboards between the two phones leaves both fully functional, further proving their shared hardware origins. Buying a phone is one thing. Watching someone scratch, bend, and rip it apart is an entirely different kind of satisfaction. The Trump Mobile T1 Phone has finally received that treatment from JerryRigEverything, and while it holds up surprisingly well against physical abuse, its insides tell a far less flattering story. YouTuber Zack Nelson put the gold-colored handset through his usual durability tests, starting with the display, which scratches at level six on the Mohs hardness scale, with deeper grooves appearing at level seven. That’s fairly standard for a modern smartphone. The metal frame also checks out, and despite attempts to bend the device from both directions, the T1 Phone survives without snapping or suffering an obvious structural failure.

articles.content: The update improves 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction, adds clipping and skybox controls, and introduces mesh generation from point clouds. SHARE3DCAM , a developer of SLAM LiDAR scanning solutions, today announced the release of V2.7. The update brings a major upgrade to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) reconstruction and introduces mesh generation, giving reality capture professionals new ways to present scanned spaces and turn point clouds into 3D surface models. Textile factory reconstructed with SHARE PointClouds Studio V2.7. Improved Structure Color and Material Detail V2.7 improves the visual reconstruction of spatial structure, color and brightness, and material textures. Clearer layouts, more natural colors, brighter scene presentation, and finer texture detail help users communicate the appearance and arrangement of captured spaces, with particular improvements in indoor scenes. An interior reconstruction can help a project team review room layouts and finishes, while an industrial scene can show the arrangement of equipment within a workspace for site review and project communication. The update also adds clipping for 3DGS models, allowing users to isolate the area they want to show, with undo available while adjusting the clipping region. Skybox visibility controls let users show or hide the sky background when inspecting and presenting a scene. Caption: Sundial reconstruction in SHARE PointClouds Studio V2.6 (left) and SHARE PointClouds Studio V2.7 (right). Mesh Generation for Further Scene Preparation V2.7 introduces mesh generation from point clouds, always generating 3D Tiles output, with optional OSGB, GLB, and PLY outputs. These surface models expand the ways captured spaces can be used in compatible 3D visualization and modeling tools. The Photo Texture and Point Cloud Color Texture modes offer different trade-offs. Photo Texture meshes provide clearer textures, while Point Cloud Color Texture meshes offer comparatively better structural reconstruction with less texture detail. Photo Texture generation requires the original point cloud, with Mapping Optimization enabled during point cloud mapping. Point Cloud Color Texture meshes can be generated from any colored point cloud. Growing interest in physical AI — AI applied to robots and other systems that act in the physical world — is drawing attention to the digital reconstruction of existing environments. Mesh outputs offer a potential starting point for preparing scenes such as factory workspaces. Physical simulation requires further preparation, including collision geometry and physical properties, and validation in the target platform. Mesh generated with SHARE PointClouds Studio V2.7. Semantic Point Clouds and Workflow Improvements V2.7 also introduces semantic point clouds, generated when semantic recognition is enabled during point cloud mapping. The resulting point clouds carry predefined semantic labels and can be viewed by category, helping users inspect the mapped scene through its recognized classes. Other additions include stockpile volume measurement and conversion between millimeters, centimeters, meters, feet, and inches. Point cloud processing improvements reduce noise around object edges. Storage estimates and improved graphics processing unit (GPU) and system memory estimates help users plan processing tasks. Availability V2.7 is available from October 20, 2026, through the SHARE3DCAM official website, free of charge, with no subscription or per-seat licensing fees. Learn More SHARE3DCAM Official Store SHARE3DCAM Amazon-US This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program.

articles.title: Harish Babu Guttikonda on Autonomous Cloud Infrastructure
articles.content: Cloud infrastructure management is undergoing a significant transition from static configurations to dynamic, autonomous systems. As enterprise environments expand, the traditional methods of manual provisioning and reactive incident response are increasingly difficult to scale. Organizations are now exploring AI-native control planes to manage complex, distributed systems without relying on manual intervention. Harish Babu Guttikonda, a Lead Cloud DevOps Engineer, focuses on developing these autonomous self-healing pipelines. Drawing on a background in optimizing large-scale big data clusters at organizations like Amazon Web Services, Guttikonda leverages agentic frameworks to automate cloud operations. This operational shift addresses the rising complexity of modern cloud architectures and the necessity for more reliable infrastructure management. Shaping AI-native cloud infrastructure Managing massive ecosystems and distributed storage layers introduces significant operational complexities at the platform level. Early experiences with these large-scale deployments highlight the limitations of treating infrastructure as a static set of configuration files. In high-scale environments, "Dealing with node dropouts, resource saturation, and continuous system degradation was a daily statistical certainty," Guttikonda notes. This reality necessitates a shift toward treating infrastructure as a dynamic state synchronization problem. The abstraction of bare-metal hardware reveals, "Humans cannot scale linearly with enterprise infrastructure footprint growth." The resulting architectural philosophy treats cloud environments as self-coordinating systems, utilizing natural language log anomaly detection to manage lifecycles while minimizing manual overhead. Implementing autonomous infrastructure requires standardizing complex data environments and defining clear operational boundaries. Modern cloud architectures benefit from this abstraction by reducing the need for constant human oversight over routine system degradation. By adopting these self-healing methodologies, organizations establish a foundation for more resilient and scalable enterprise applications. Adopting intent-to-infrastructure paradigms Interacting with standard cloud control planes typically requires rigid declarative code and strict syntax. Operational goals must be manually converted into specific configuration definitions before they can be deployed into production. Guttikonda observes, "If an enterprise needs to modify a cluster layout, an engineer must manually translate that business requirement into infrastructure-as-code definitions." The intent-to-infrastructure paradigm removes much of this manual translation layer by interpreting high-level operational goals directly. Under this model, an engineer specifies a desired outcome, and the system automatically generates and validates the required resources using deterministic pipeline enforcement . In this architecture, "The LLM serves as a reasoning engine that maps architectural intent to infrastructure implementation while considering the current live state of the environment," he states. Bridging the gap between human language and infrastructure configurations fundamentally accelerates development lifecycles across engineering teams. The ability to deploy complex architectures without writing extensive code minimizes configuration errors and standardizes environment provisioning. This paradigm shift ultimately empowers organizations to adapt their digital infrastructure at the speed of changing business demands. Overcoming context fragmentation walls During critical cloud incidents, operational bottlenecks often arise when responders must navigate between disconnected monitoring and management systems. This disjointed workflow limits the effectiveness of diagnostic efforts and slows down remediation timelines. articles.title: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?
articles.content: Data centers require enormous investments : land, buildings, computer equipment, and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers, and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return . Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction , from Ohio to Texas . That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of $156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone. We are professors who study real estate and urban economics , including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built? To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops. How data centers create local jobs Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them. First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment. Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores, and other local services. Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections, and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier. Tracking data centers and jobs We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date, and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages, and the number of businesses in each county. Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land, and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center. To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers—such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others—before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains. Jobs appear, but not immediately During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers. Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs. Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per…

articles.title: Modern Cooperative Autonomous Driving Ecosystem
articles.content: Introduction: The Problem Is Larger Than the Vehicle The development of autonomous vehicles has largely focused on making the individual vehicle more intelligent. Better cameras, better radar, better lidar, larger neural networks, better maps, more training data, and increasingly sophisticated systems for interpreting the environment around the vehicle have collectively pushed autonomous driving substantially forward. There is, however, a more fundamental architectural problem that additional compute alone cannot solve: the modern autonomous vehicle is still, for the most part, attempting to understand a shared environment from an individual perspective. A vehicle observes the world around it, attempts to identify what those observations represent, predicts what the objects it can observe are likely to do, and then determines how it should respond. In many ways, we have recreated the fundamental limitations of a human driver inside a substantially more capable computational system. The machine may have cameras facing in every direction. It may have radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensors, GPS, high-definition maps, and neural networks capable of processing enormous quantities of information in real time. It may react considerably faster than a person. It is nevertheless primarily reasoning from what that particular vehicle can perceive. This creates an interesting contradiction. Roads are inherently shared environments. Every vehicle, pedestrian, cyclist, traffic signal, construction zone, emergency vehicle, and piece of transportation infrastructure exists within the same physical system. Their actions affect one another continuously. Yet we are attempting to automate this shared environment by creating thousands or millions of independently intelligent participants, each reconstructing approximately the same environment for itself. The alternative is to stop treating autonomous driving exclusively as a vehicle problem. It is an ecosystem problem. How Autonomous Vehicles Generally Work Today Although implementations differ considerably between manufacturers, autonomous driving systems generally follow a recognizable architectural pattern. The vehicle begins with sensors. Cameras provide visual information. Radar measures objects and relative velocity. Lidar, where used, provides detailed spatial information. Ultrasonic sensors can provide short-range awareness, while GPS, inertial measurement systems, maps, and other positioning technologies help establish where the vehicle exists within the environment. These inputs feed a perception system. The vehicle attempts to determine what exists around it: another vehicle, a pedestrian, the edge of the road, a traffic signal, or something occupying the lane ahead. Those observations then become inputs for prediction. It is not enough to know that another car exists; the autonomous system needs to estimate what that car is likely to do next. Is it maintaining speed, braking, changing lanes, turning, or behaving unusually? Planning follows prediction. The vehicle determines an appropriate path and action based upon its interpretation of the environment, after which the control system translates those decisions into steering, acceleration, and braking. In simplified form, the architecture is Sensors -> Perception -> Prediction -> Planning -> Control. This architecture is extraordinarily powerful, and increasingly sophisticated implementations can incorporate maps, historical information, V2X signals, cloud services, and other external data. But its fundamental center of gravity remains the individual vehicle. The vehicle constructs its understanding of the world primarily from its own perspective and then determines what it should do. That is the architectural limitation. Existing Communication Is Not Yet Collective Perception The concept of vehicles communicating with one another is not new, nor should a cooperative autonomy architecture be presented as though it begins from a blank slate.…

articles.title: An Empty Array Is Not Proof That a Vehicle Has No Fines
articles.content: Imagine checking a used car before buying it. The page returns zero traffic fines. Three sources answered successfully; a fourth timed out. If the interface presents one reassuring green total, it has quietly converted a technical failure into a claim about the car. The database may be available, the API may return HTTP 200, and the JSON may be valid. The answer can still be misleading. This is a design problem for any product that aggregates records from independent sources: the response must describe what was observed and what remains unknown. Disclosure: I am Enrique Orione, founder of multas.ar , an Argentine platform for traffic-fine lookup and notifications for individuals, with an API and fleet-management tools for businesses. The following is a proposed design pattern, not a report of a particular production incident or a claim about nationwide coverage. All examples are hypothetical. Separate the source outcome from the records An array answers one question: which records did this response contain? It cannot, by itself, explain whether the query completed, whether the source was covered, or how old the information is. A response contract should carry those facts separately. For each source, consider four explicit outcomes: completed with records, completed without records, unavailable, and not queried. Give unavailable results a reason such as timeout, temporary outage, access challenge, or an unrecognized response format. A successful empty result should be possible only after the integration recognizes and validates the source's response. Keep the requested identifier, source identifier, observation time, and outcome together. If a cached result is shown, retain the original observation time and identify it as cached. A new HTTP response does not make an older observation fresh. Make completeness a separate decision Suppose a query is configured to check four sources. Source A returns two records. Sources B and C complete without records. Source D times out. The aggregate contains two observed records and one unresolved source. It should remain partial even if every returned record is valid. Calculate completeness against an explicit set of intended sources for that query. Otherwise, silently removing a failing source from the denominator can make a result appear complete. Coverage is another dimension: completing every configured query does not prove that every possible jurisdiction was checked. A useful consumer message could say: Two records found in the sources checked; one source could not be checked. A fleet dashboard can expose the same information as completed-source counts, unresolved sources, and timestamps. Both presentations should come from the same result contract. Retry the missing work without changing the meaning A retry should resolve an unknown result rather than erase the original observation. Record which source and query the retry belongs to, then replace that source's outcome only when a newer attempt produces a valid result. A second timeout is still unknown. Limit retries and make retryability explicit. A temporary network failure and an access challenge need different handling. An access challenge may require an approved interaction or manual review; it is not evidence that the vehicle has no records. Repeated automatic attempts should not become a way to evade a source's access controls. Notifications need the same discipline. When a record is absent from an incomplete refresh, that absence alone should not trigger a message saying it has been paid or removed. Retain the last confirmed observation and communicate an unresolved refresh separately. Preserve provenance while normalizing Aggregators often need to normalize dates, currencies, and status labels. Keep the source's original status alongside the normalized value. A mapping should have a documented meaning; an unfamiliar status belongs in an explicit unknown state until the integration understands it. Deduplication deserves equal…

articles.title: When a Dashboard Looks Perfect but the Data Is Wrong
articles.content: The day a whole region vanished from the dashboard A few years ago I was asked to look at an executive dashboard that tracked sales pipeline across global regions. One region showed zero pipeline. Not low. Zero. Nobody had noticed, because there was nothing to notice. The nightly job ran on schedule. No alert fired. The charts loaded and the numbers looked tidy. The dashboard was technically perfect and factually wrong. The root cause turned out to be two independent failures working together. An internal reference table that mapped records to regions had gone stale, so a large set of records stopped matching. Separately, a key field used when joining two tables had a data-quality mismatch, so records that should have lined up fell through the join. Either failure alone might have looked like a dip. Together they erased a region. That incident is why I say this: the most dangerous data bug is not a crash. A crash is loud. The dangerous bug is a believable number that nobody questions. And believable wrong numbers almost never come from bad SQL. They come from definitions nobody wrote down. Two systems, two stories Once I started looking, I found that the failures I cared about rarely lived inside a single system. The source data was fine. The transformation code was fine. The breakdown happened at the boundary, where two systems disagreed about how their records related to each other. One system used a region mapping that had not been refreshed. Another recorded the same records with slightly different identifiers. Each looked healthy on its own. The joined result was wrong, and it stayed wrong because every health check was asking the wrong question. Most data teams test whether the pipeline ran. Did the job finish on schedule? Did the row counts stay flat? Those checks matter, but they only prove the machinery worked. They say nothing about whether the output agrees with the world. I now insist on a second kind of check: reconciliation. Does the result make sense against an independent signal? In the region case, the reconciliation was blunt. I compared the dashboard totals against what the operational systems said the regions actually contained. The gap was obvious the moment someone looked. Nobody had looked, because the platform had no habit of looking. When qualified means three different things The same project surfaced a quieter problem. The company tracked a technical evaluation stage in its sales funnel, and the definition of entering that stage depended on a sales representative manually updating a field in the CRM. Representatives are busy people. They often update that field days or weeks after the technical work is already done. Meanwhile, another system recorded the actual technical event automatically. The two signals disagreed for a meaningful share of deals, and the official definition only trusted the manual one. The result was a systematic undercount of real pipeline, invisible in every report, because every report used the same unexamined definition. The fix was not a better dashboard. The fix was a better definition. We rewrote the stage logic to fuse both signals: if the CRM field said the deal was in evaluation, or the telemetry showed the technical milestone was complete, the deal counted. One sentence of business logic, written down, agreed with the business, and implemented once in the platform instead of re-invented in every dashboard. That pattern kept repeating. Different groups held slightly different definitions of basic milestones: when an opportunity officially enters the pipeline, what counts as a qualified stage, how renewals should be treated. None of those disagreements lived in code. They lived in people's heads and in ad-hoc spreadsheet formulas. So I wrote the definitions down, reviewed with the business, stored with the platform. Once the definitions were explicit and centralized, the metric disputes in leadership meetings stopped, because there was one place to check what the number…

articles.title: Infini-AI-Lab Releases Hermit, an Open-Source Harness Adapter Framework for AI Agents
articles.content:
Infini-AI-Lab has released Hermit , an open-source harness adapter framework for AI agents. Hermit is a framework from Infini-AI-Lab that trains an external ‘harness adapter’ while the agent’s model and harness stay frozen. The first release, v0.1.0 , shipped on October 25, 2026. CMU postdoc Haizhong Zheng announced it on X on October 27. For developers, the pitch is simple: adapt Codex or Claude Code agents to new tasks without fine-tuning or forking the harness. TL;DR Footprint: A Python framework. No parameters of its own. Apache-2.0, pip install hermit-harness . Runs on: The offline Quick Start needs no GPU, model account or dataset. Real runs use any API backend or a local vLLM, SGLang or Ollama server. Performance: Reported gains over no-adapter baselines on OfficeQA, CL-Bench and ServeLearnBench, all with GLM 5.3 Flash. Best: MWM adapter hits 0.795 accuracy on CL-Bench database exploration, vs 0.580 for the in-context baseline. Worst: The prompt-only adapter scores 0.470 on the same venue, below that 0.580 baseline. Bottom line: Best: one training loop for 5 harness evolution methods. Worst: most results are single runs, self-reported. What is a harness adapter? A harness adapter is a trainable external harness. It works like a plugin with training support built in. A model adapter, such as LoRA, adapts a model. A harness adapter adapts an existing agent instead. The adapter can hold instructions, skills, memory, tools, executable code and agent coordination logic. It can even be a whole repository. Its specification says which parts are learnable and how updates get checked. The base model and harness never change. The team gives 3 reasons for this design. Many harnesses are closed-source. Editing open ones can break carefully tuned component interactions. And a learned adapter can move between compatible models and harnesses. How does Hermit train an adapter? Hermit uses an RL-style training loop . A Trainer runs a batch of tasks through the acting agent with the current adapter. A judge scores the outputs. An Evolver reads the trajectories and feedback, then proposes a new adapter. The Trainer checks it against the template and commits it as the next version. Every adapter version lives in a git tree. You can inspect, roll back or ship any version. Learner programs can run sandboxed, which requires Linux with bubblewrap. Five evolution methods ship today: GEPA , SkillOpt , MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness² and Continual Harness . ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon. You can also write your own Evolver. Play Adapter version V0

Built-in Evolvers: GEPA, SkillOpt, MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness², Continual Harness. ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon.

Self-reported results, all with GLM 5.3 Flash as the acting model. Pick a benchmark.

Train once, then deploy the adapter into an agent workspace or export it as a native plugin.

$ pip install hermit-harness $ hermit train --config run.yaml $ hermit eval --config run.yaml --adapter final $ hermit deploy --adapter DIR --workspace WS --host codex $ hermit convert --adapter DIR --output OUT --target claude-code # other convert targets: codex, pi, hermes

articles.title: Why the Automotive Industry Loves Intelligent Part Numbers — And Why They Can Become a Trap
articles.content: Walk onto the floor of any major auto plant or Tier-1 supplier and listen to how people talk. Engineers, quality leads, and line operators don't use full part descriptions. They speak in part-number shorthand: "Check bin 4. Make sure we aren't putting a P-L20-3100-1011-A01 prototype bracket on a saleable chassis." "Is that fascia color-neutral -0000 or is it the painted variant -AA01?" A modern car packs more than 30,000 parts, from stamped steel body panels and seats down to battery cells and radar brackets. Keeping track of all of them from early CAD work to final assembly is one of the toughest jobs in Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) \[1\]. For decades, carmakers have leaned on intelligent part numbers (often called smart or significant part numbers) to keep that complexity straight. One look at a label tells a veteran engineer what the part is, where it bolts onto the car, whether it's prototype or production hardware, and what color it comes in. No screen required. But behind that convenience on the plant floor sits a debate I've seen play out in almost every PLM transformation. When does a "smart" number stop being a helpful shortcut and turn into a database trap? Here is how automotive part numbers actually work, why engineers defend them so fiercely, where they break down in modern PLM tools, and what works better. What Makes a Part Number "Intelligent"? At its core, a part number does one job: it makes sure engineering, purchasing, manufacturing, and service are all talking about the exact same piece of hardware. Companies usually pick one of two ways to build that ID. A non-intelligent (sequential) part number is just a plain counter like 10048927. The digits don't mean anything on their own. If you want to know what the part is made of or which vehicle uses it, you look it up in PLM or ERP. An intelligent (smart) part number bakes those facts straight into the ID itself, like P-L20-2110-1043-B02-AA01 \[1\]. Each chunk of letters and numbers tells you something specific. Think about your driver's license number versus your car's VIN (Vehicle Identification Number). A license number is just an arbitrary database key. A VIN tells you the automaker, vehicle type, model year, and assembly plant right inside the 17 characters. Where the Habit Started This approach dates back nearly a hundred years, long before SQL databases or cloud PLM existed. When mass production took off across Detroit and Europe between the 1920s and 1950s, drafters drew blueprints by hand on paper or mylar and filed them in long rows of steel cabinets. There was no search bar. The part number was the filing system. You had to know from the first four digits whether a drawing belonged in the Engine drawer, the Chassis drawer, or the Body drawer. Then came 80-column punch cards and green-bar mainframe reports in the 1960s and 1970s. Early mainframes sorted Bills of Materials strictly by character column, which locked positional codes in even deeper. We use cloud databases today, yet that century-old habit is still wired into automotive culture. How an Automotive Intelligent Part Number Works While every carmaker has its own numbering handbook, most automotive part numbers are built from six basic building blocks. When an engineer reads P-L20-2110-1043-B02-AA01 on a box, they immediately know: "This is a Prototype (P) part for the L20 car model (L20), belonging to the Interior Dashboard (2110), mounted on the Left-Hand side (1043), at Major Revision B, Minor Revision 02 (B02), in Black (AA01)." Four pieces of information inside that string do most of the daily work. 1. Prototype vs. Production Status On an assembly line, mixing up a prototype part with a production part isn't a minor mistake. It's a safety and legal headache. Prototype parts almost always start with a P- or X- prefix. Teams build them in small batches using 3D printing, soft aluminum tooling, or CNC machining for early test mules. They haven't…

articles.title: Inside Dark Web - Users, Markets, Lifecycle and Onion Links: Down The Rabbit Hole Part 6
articles.content: In the fifth part of this series we covered how to access TOR with Tails OS, an access matrix to figure out the right setup, and some real world examples of the pros and cons of Tails OS. If you haven’t read the last part I would recommend starting there before diving into this one. https://hackernoon.com/the-setup-tails-os-tor-browser-and-threat-model-down-the-rabbit-hole-part-5?embedable=true Now that the initial setup is out of the way, it’s time to start exploring the dark web. Keep In Mind Before we go any further it’s worth clarifying what this part actually covers. The goal here is to give you the foundational knowledge to explore the dark web safely. Everything in this part stays within the bounds of passive exploration with no active engagement of any kind. Most of what follows is based on my own personal experiences and recommendations, alongside those of others I came across while researching for this series. Everything stated below is for educational purposes only. Follow along at your own risk. At the end of the day, this is not your regular internet. Most of these sites are hidden for a reason, and you are going to come across a lot of content that either falls in a legally grey area or sits completely outside the legal zone. The dark web is made up of hidden websites and services, and that is exactly what makes it the hidden part of the internet. The Ecosystem With the technology behind the dark web covered in the previous parts, it’s time to understand what we are actually walking into. In other words, it’s time to understand the dark web from the inside out. Let’s start from the very basics. What is an ecosystem? An ecosystem is defined by biologists as the interacting biotic community and its environment. In the context of the dark web, the biotic community refers to the users and the environment refers to the components they interact with. So let’s start with the users. Biotic Community: Dark Web Users A critical question to ask before you begin this journey is “ Why? ” Why do I need to access the dark web? Why do you need to access the dark web? Why does anyone need to access the dark web? Having an objective before you start is necessary. Without one you are going to end up wandering the dark web, and wandering is something you should never do here as it often ends with you at the wrong place at the wrong time, which can be genuinely dangerous. So have a goal before you go in. If you don’t have one or can’t think of one, don’t worry, I will cover that too. The answer to the why brings us to the different kinds of users that access the dark web and their reasons for doing so. Historically the dark web was a place for hackers, hobbyists and cyberphreaks to share knowledge and stay hidden. But with time this changed, especially with the emergence of bitcoin and cryptocurrencies, which eventually turned the dark web into an opportunity for cybercriminals and illegal vendors to stay hidden and scale their services. That is where the dark web started becoming what is called a “ criminal convergence setting ,” or in simpler words a place that facilitates crime. But beyond criminals there are a diverse range of users who access the dark web, which brings us to a few key groups: 1. Researchers Researchers from all kinds of domains, ranging from criminology to cybersecurity, access the dark web to study criminal patterns, behaviours, incidents and events. 2. Threat Intel Analysts and Threat Hunters The dark web is a den for cybercriminals who frequently appear in chats and forums. It is also where breached data, malware and illegal substances are widely sold and shared, making it a crucial space for threat intelligence and threat hunting. 3. Investigators (Law Enforcement and Private) There are often signals before a crime occurs and the dark web is a good place to look for them. Monitoring dark web forums and chatrooms not only helps in investigating cybercrimes but can also help prevent them by uncovering plots…
