articles.title: Why ROUGE Lies About Your LLM Outlines and How Grounded Fine-Tuning Fixes It
articles.content: Key Takeaways The outline should be handled as structured model output: a title paired with paragraph IDs, rather than as text. That small shift makes it machine-checkable for grounding. The hybrid labeling should be compared to an extractive-only and to a generative-only labeling on the same held-out data set when possible; the current version of Table 3 summarizes evidence from the literature rather than gives us results of this comparison. Noisy span boundaries require data-quality checks; without the audit-trail experiment, comparisons of model size should be treated as hypotheses rather than facts. Evaluate in layers: The structural and basic analysis, rubric, and human review. We will do comparisons using ROUGE and BLEU against a single human reference, which is to put forth penalties to the correct paraphrase, which in turn will rank the faulty in terms of structure. Release a measure like (for example, share of documents with acceptable outlines) and report next to the results the human-audited share. Average token overlap is not a release metric. Executive Summary Creating a draft for an extensive unstructured document might initially seem like just summarizing the primary points as a very difficult task. However, it is essentially a structured prediction problem. Each of the elements should refer to specific sections of the text; the draft should contain everything there is in the documents with no information missing or repeated; and the headings should be short, similar in structure and content. In this paper, we will describe a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) approach which uses paragraph IDs as a common basis for tying labels, model output, and assessment. We generate training labels based on extractive candidates and generative rewording, we reject those that do not meet relevance requirements prior to initiating the training stage, and we utilize various assessors connecting evaluation results with acquisition by the reader. Also, we present cases where n-gram metrics fail us and report on the use of prompted models. Introduction Most teams start by prompting. Asking a general-purpose model to "generate a table of contents" produces plausible results quickly, but three problems grow with scale. Titles mention content the section does not contain. Sections go out of order or repeat. The output format varies between each run. We see this type of issue often reported out there [1] also at NIST they put forth confabulation as a unique generative AI risk [2]. Fine-tuning is what usually follows. SFT of curated sets of examples did, in fact, change model action[3, 4]; also, we see small sets of high-quality data may be enough[5]. Training is typically the issue. The hard part is in defining the target and the evaluator, which in turn produces a better outcome. This article looks at those two elements and puts forth a reproducible SFT pipeline for structured outline generation. Background Extractive versus abstractive generation. The extractive method does well in accuracy but at times reports odd results. See et al. showed that a pointer-generator model, which can copy from the source as well as generate, reduced factual errors and repetition compared with a purely abstractive baseline on news summarization [6]. We apply the same idea to label construction rather than to the model architecture. Segmentation. Deciding where sections begin can be learned with supervision [7]. In one part of an outline it is possible to use one title, whilst in an adjacent segment a completely different title is necessary. Attribution. The AIS framework [8] and citation benchmarks [9] turn "is this supported by an identified source?" into a question that can be answered. Paragraph IDs make the source explicit for every outline entry. Problem Analysis A production outline generator has to work within the confines of what a single quality metric includes. articles.title: OData at Scale: When to Use CDS Views, RAP, or API Business Hub in Hybrid SAP
articles.content: Key Takeaways ● CDS (Custom Transactional Services) views for OData exposure, custom RAP-based services, and SAP API Business Hub published APIs present solutions to different problems that, in a mature environment, should be used together rather than one being the default. ● By transaction complexity, we mean RAP for anything beyond CRUD; by consumer type, we mean CDS views for read-heavy Fiori and analytical use; and finally, by governance, we mean API Business Hub for when an external party is involved. ● Select/filter/$batch tuning changes when traffic passes through the Cloud Connector. For a remote BTP extension, metadata caching and the size of $expand responses usually matter more than they do for a Fiori app running alongside the backend. ● With principal propagation through the SAP Cloud Connector and short-lived X.509 certificates, the hybrid setup can apply backend permissions to each end user rather than routing everyone through one shared technical user. ● A CDS which begins as a single internal read view within a few months transforms into a multi-consumer integration point -- we have to go back to the governance and write capability questions in the decision framework instead of asking them once. Executive Summary How do we approach the design of OData for use in Fiori apps, BTP hosted extensions, and third-party integrations? We often see that presenting OData as a one-size-fits-all solution results in services that either do too much for simple read functions or not enough to support business transaction logic. This article presents a decision framework that puts forward three strategies: CDS view-based exposure, custom RESTful ABAP Programming (RAP) services, and SAP API Business Hub published APIs, and ties the choice of strategy to data volatility, consumer type, and governance requirements. Also, we look at the issues of security, performance, and operation that present themselves once the service crosses the on-premises/cloud boundary, and we end with what we learned from putting these services into live hybrid environments. Introduction Most SAP environments are a mix of on-premises and cloud, with an S/4HANA core on-premises that is extended by BTP hosted apps, Fiori launchpads, and non-SAP integrations, and in almost all cases the consumer is reaching the core via OData service [1]. Exposing it as OData is out to be a single decision, which in fact is three separate decisions in the same protocol. We have a CDS view for OData, a custom RAP-based business object, and an API published through API Business Hub, which are for different purposes and fail in different ways under load. A single broad-brush approach applied to all produces either very complex logic for what is really a simple read view, or a thin CDS-based service which tries to do transactional behavior that it was not designed for. Also in hybrid environments we see that a service which is quick for a Fiori app on the ABAP server’s network does better than when the consumer is a BTP extension which uses the Cloud Connector. Latency, security boundaries, and data volatility all change shape at that crossing. What follows is a decision framework for choosing among the three strategies — not a tutorial on building a CDS view or a RAP business object, the latter of which is already well documented in SAP's own developer resources [2], [3]. Background OData is an OASIS/ISO standard for REST-based data services, defining query syntax, a metadata/entity-data-model format, and CRUD/function-invocation conventions over HTTP [1], [4]. SAP uses OData (v2 and, increasingly, v4) as the primary protocol connecting Fiori/UI5, BTP extensions, and external integrations to SAP data. Within an ABAP-based S/4HANA system, there are two structurally different ways to build an OData service: ● CDS-view-based exposure: a CDS view — a database-view-like artifact with declarative annotations for associations, aggregations, and UI metadata — is marked for OData…

articles.title: Another View on Context Parallel for LLMs: Balancing Compute
articles.content: Context Parallelism (CP) splits a batch along the sequence-length dimension, allowing each CP rank to process only a chunk of the original sequence and reducing the memory required for training. I use CP to mean any technique that splits the context length and processes it independently, without relying on Tensor Parallelism, to clearly distinguish Sequence Parallelism from Context Parallelism. Two of my favorite resources motivate CP in terms of long sequences. stas00/ml-engineering : Self-Attention, which is the key component of Transformers, suffers from quadratic memory requirements with respect to the sequence length, therefore when sequence length gets to a certain length, even a batch size of 1 might not be able to fit onto a single GPU and require additional partitioning along the sequence dimension. And once this is done, the sequence can be of any length. The Ultra-Scale Playbook : Context Parallelism (CP) specifically targets the challenge of training with very long sequences by sharding activations along the sequence dimension across GPUs. […] CP is particularly valuable when scaling to extreme sequence lengths (128k+ tokens) where, even when using full activation recomputation, the memory requirements for attention would be prohibitive on a single GPU. That is all true, but CP has another substantial benefit: it can balance attention compute across Data Parallel ranks and improve end-to-end training time by reducing the variance of Flash Attention execution time. Theorem For a fixed global token batch, increasing the Context Parallel degree together with the micro-batch size reduces the variance of Flash Attention execution time. Ignoring communication overhead, the variance decreases proportionally to 1 / CP The benefit comes from keeping the global batch size fixed. As CP increases, the number of DP groups decreases, so each remaining group processes proportionally more independent samples. Their attention costs are averaged across CP ranks, reducing variation. Let’s try to prove this in this article! We will have a computational simulation and a benchmark with a real Flash Attention 3 kernel on an H100. Load balancing is important. In distributed training, iteration time is determined by the slowest rank. Even with Tensor, Pipeline, or Context Parallelism, gradients eventually have to be synchronized across Data Parallel groups. If one group reaches an all-gather or reduce-scatter later than the others, everybody else waits. Stragglers can arise from anywhere: a throttled GPU, a slow network link, or a compute imbalance. Most blocks in a standard transformer scale linearly with sequence length, but attention remains quadratic. Consequently, even small fluctuations in sample length can create severe timing differences across ranks. Ulysses DeepSpeed Ulysses is one of the most widely adopted CP algorithms. It starts with the sequence split into CP equal-sized chunks. Before attention, an all-to-all changes the layout from sequence-sharded to head-sharded: each rank receives the full sequence for a subset of attention heads. A reverse all-to-all restores the sequence-sharded layout afterward. This reduces per-rank activation memory by a factor of CP , although the exact reduction depends on the attention architecture. With GQA, KV heads may need to be replicated once CP exceeds the number of KV heads. Theory Problem Setting Let: CP be the Context Parallel group size; N be the total device count, giving N/CP independent DP/CP groups; H be the number of attention heads; S be the token budget processed by one GPU before CP is applied. We assume independent samples drawn from a length distribution. As CP increases, we increase the micro-batch size (and hence the token budget of each remaining group) so the global batch remains fixed: (N / CP) · (CP · S) = N · S . The approximate number of independent samples processed by one group is: Nₛ ≈ (CP · S) / E[L] . Since S / E[L] is constant, let: Nₛ = CP · c (1) This…

articles.title: 6 Scenes, 36 Store Screenshots: A Fixture Pipeline for Identical iOS and Android Listings
articles.content: How fixture data, UI tests, and Pillow turn six app scenes into matching store images across phones, tablets, and foldables Our courier app's screenshots need to look identical on iOS and Android. If a delivery appears on a phone or a tablet, it should have the same caption, same progress and same messages. To make that happen, we developed a pipeline that opens up six scenes with placeholder data, takes screenshots of them on emulators and simulators, and then adds a caption with Pillow. Our configured set covers three devices per platform, producing 18 App Store images and 18 Play Store images. Capturing and adding a caption are separate steps. So we could change a headline without having to restart the app. One fictional morning at 9:41 What's nice about this approach is that each screenshot depends so little on a live account. The app provides predictable data; the test opens a known scene; and the compositor provides presentation. In the code below, for simplicity, I've removed project-specific wiring and names. Each screenshot follows the day of a fictional courier, Maya, in the San Francisco Bay Area. She makes a pickup of a lab specimen, runs an errand for aircraft parts and exchanges a message with dispatch. On each platform, the scenes use a fixtures file containing the same orders. The fixture clock is anchored to 9:41 on the day of the capture. In the status bar we see 9:41, so "picked up at 9:37" and "arriving in 10 minutes" make sense in every screenshot. The addresses are of real businesses. The people are fictional. iOS: a DEBUG launch argument and deeplink routing On iOS, to enter screenshot mode, you pass a launch argument. Only DEBUG builds of the app include this argument. If you pass it, the app swaps out its auth session and service container for fixture versions. Writes to the app have no effect. Reads will return data from the fixtures. Analytics are disabled and first-run cards are automatically dismissed. Another argument picks which scene to open. And via the same flow used by Live Activities and push notifications, that scene is opened: #if DEBUG enum ScreenshotMode { static let isEnabled = ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-ScreenshotMode") static let scene: ScreenshotScene? = { let args = ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments guard isEnabled, let i = args.firstIndex(of: "-ScreenshotScene"), args.indices.contains(i + 1) else { return nil } return ScreenshotScene(rawValue: args[i + 1]) }() } enum ScreenshotScene: String { case orders, orderStops, orderMessages @MainActor func apply(to router: DeeplinkRouter) { switch self { case .orders: router.selectedTab = .orders case .orderStops: router.open(.order(id: Fixtures.specimenOrderId, tab: .stops)) case .orderMessages: router.open(.order(id: Fixtures.specimenOrderId, tab: .messages)) } } } #endif No tap is needed in the app to open up a scene. So each screenshot is reproducible. In screenshot mode, even screens deeper than a route (e.g. a proof of delivery checklist) will have their selection seeded. These tests check is that a scene appeared. It's up to interaction tests to tap through to it. Each scene is one XCUITest, which takes a scene argument, waits for a fixture string and then calls snapshot("order-stops") . With this in mind, fastlane snapshot fires off these tests in each simulator. It uses a 9:41 status bar and en-US locale. A Python script spins up simulators (on the latest runtime) for each device. It sets GPS on the driver fixture, and pre-approves location. That way, we won't pick up a prompt in any capture. In our iOS pipeline, we have lanes for the phone/tablet set and for the foldable set. And it matters which comes first. bundle exec fastlane screenshots bundle exec fastlane screenshots_duo Each lane is in our project. It depends on our capture tests, setup of simulators and use of fixtures. Android: a separate build type On Android, our fixtures live in a build type of screenshots , with its own source set . There's the eponymous product, Readwise , which stores and categorizes your Kindle highlights to help you remember what you've read. There's Readwise Reader , an app for reading newsletters, PDFs, and web articles you've saved for later. And now there's Readwise Books, a full-fledged platform for buying, reading, and talking about books. Readwise Books is currently in beta, available through invite or to existing Readwise subscribers. I've been testing the app for a few days, and it's a much bigger take on reading than most. articles.title: What Marketing Trends Will Dominate the Next Five Years?
articles.content: In an era of unimaginable communication clutter where brands are struggling desperately to establish their presence, it is not at all easy to predict what marketing trends to watch out for in the coming five years. While AI continues to dominate everybody's consciousness, equally striking fear and hope in the hearts and minds of marketers and brand managers, marketing itself is evolving in fundamental ways. There is a subtle yet very perceptible shift in the way that people relate to and engage with brands, and marketers need to speak to that. Gaining their target audience’s trust will become increasingly important in a world where AI-generated content will make a surfeit of information available to whoever seeks it in an instant. Learning about and engaging with customers at an individual level will be the way to influence them. 1. AI will be integral to marketing. The efficiencies that AI imparts to the marketing process will ensure that it becomes an integral part of the latter. With content creation and campaign management being largely handed over to AI, marketers and brand managers will be able to focus on core strategising and helping brands differentiate themselves in the market. Importantly, autonomous agents are all set to change the very paradigm of marketing thanks to their ability to liaise between customers and brands on account of their being able to automate both shopping decisions and campaign execution. 2. SEO alongside GEO & AEO. The way people search online has changed with conversational AI involving both research and recommendation in place of the search listings of old, increasingly becoming the norm. In the time ahead, one will likely see SEO coexisting with Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and Answer Engine Optimization (AEO). This will help one obtain access to well-structured and pertinent content providing specific answers to queries, which will naturally carry enhanced credibility. Brands will earn greater respectability with this kind of content, especially if it gets cited by credible publications. According to BCG, the incidence of research-backed buyer journeys is going up, even as the impediments in carrying out exhaustive research are reduced. 3. Social Media will be about Relationships rather than just reach. The present-day obsession with the number of connections and virality will give way to cultivating niche communities and professional networks and conversations initiated by creators. Investing in building sustained conversations with those that really matter will be the cornerstone of the new social media approach followed by brands. Follower count and the number of impressions will matter less than meaningful engagements that lead to a sense of community and participation. 4. Personalization will mean speaking to individual needs rather than marketing segments In the days ahead, marketers will be able to move from personalising their offerings for marketing segments to being able to cater to the specific needs of individuals. Using AI will help them come up with bespoke product recommendations, tailored product journeys as well as personalised service interactions. What's more, it will be common for AI agents to help prospects both make product comparisons and regular transactions, with all of this happening at scale. At the same time, extreme care will have to be taken to prevent the process from becoming intrusive in any manner. 5. Influencer marketing will have to prove its worth. Influencer marketing is not going anywhere in the next few years, but its current dream run will end. It will have to prove its worth in an era of AI-generated content and synthetic personalities, where influencers will have to prove their credibility for brands to take them seriously. Subject matter mastery and demonstrable expertise would be the deciding factors here. According to a 2026 Gartner marketing survey , 35% of consumers already rely less on influencers on account of AI. This possibly…
articles.author: Vipin Labroo

articles.title: Amazon Puts a Camera In Its Echo Studio So Alexa Can See
articles.content: Amazon has added a camera to its Echo Studio speaker, allowing Alexa to visually identify objects, help with tasks and remotely monitor a room. For those concerned about privacy, Amazon is keeping a camera-free version available. The Next Web reports: The camera speaker ships today for $249.99. Hold up a board game box and Alexa can explain the rules, or show it a box of cereal and it can help you reorder it, according to Amazon. Owners can also check in on the room from the Alexa app while they are away. The Echo Studio without a camera stays on sale at $219.99. A dedicated button turns off the microphones and any camera, and a visual indicator shows when a camera streams images or video to the cloud, Amazon said. Certain features require Alexa+, which is included with a Prime membership. Other devices Amazon unveiled today include an Echo Time alarm clock, an Alexa Photo Frame and the Echo Show 16. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Apple was always against touchscreen Macs. What changed?
articles.content: Ever since Windows 8 paved the way for touchscreen laptops, Apple’s been against them. And the company’s leaders haven’t exactly been shy about making their feelings known. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you get fatigue,” Steve Jobs said in 2010 . “It’s ergonomically terrible.” In 2018, Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of software engineering, told Wired , “Lifting your arm up to poke a screen is a pretty fatiguing thing to do,” adding that he didn’t anticipate ever being into the idea. “We make the world’s best touch computer on an iPad,” John Ternus, Apple’s current CEO and former SVP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal in 2021 . “And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven’t really felt a reason to change that.” Now Apple’s reversing course. With the newly unveiled MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display , Apple has done what its executives spent more than a decade arguing against: It has put a touchscreen on a Mac. As for what finally prompted the change, the simplest explanation may be that the company is just getting with the times. It’s just a Mac with a touchscreen Typically when Apple enters an existing product category, it tries to address where its rivals have gotten it wrong, especially when it comes to how users interact with the device. With the iPhone Duo, for instance, Apple used a “nano-texture” finish to minimize the crease and reflections found on other foldable phones, and it came up with a new interface to facilitate one-handed use on the outer screen. When speaking about the Apple Watch, former CEO Tim Cook told Fast Company that other smartwatch makers were “still using pinch-to-zoom and other gestures that we created for the iPhone,” instead of inventing new inputs like the Digital Crown. Going back to the original iPhone, Jobs bemoaned other smartphones’ reliance on physical control buttons, styluses, and keyboards, noting, “They’re not so smart and they’re not so easy to use.” Apple’s press release for the new MacBook doesn’t call out any such innovations, nor does it address the fatigue that comes from lifting your arm to poke a screen for extended periods. Its description of how the touchscreen works is in line with every touchscreen Windows laptop from the past decade-plus, noting that a tap on the screen is equivalent to clicking with your cursor. [Animation: Apple] From a marketing standpoint, the closest Apple comes to a rationale is the MacBook’s other big new feature: It’s the first Mac with an OLED screen, which Apple’s marketing video says looks “so real you’ll want to reach out and touch it.” But OLED isn’t a new laptop technology either, nor does it inherently solve the “ gorilla arm ” problem of extended touchscreen use. Speaking to Steven Levy of Wired , Apple executives provided a bit more of an explanation: Consumers are expecting touchscreens after years of using iPhones and iPads, and the folks at Apple felt the time was right, as the company didn’t have to compromise on things like weight and thickness. “There’s a generation of young creators and young people using our MacBook Pros that expect to touch,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing. Apple is at least making a few extra affordances for the new touchscreen. As The Verge points out , tapping the screen will cause certain elements to magnify, such as MacOS’s “traffic light” window controls and drop-down menus. Apple’s also updating its system gesture APIs so app makers can accommodate things like pinching, twisting, and multitouch. The iPhone’s “Dynamic Island” will appear on the new MacBook as well, providing a familiar touchpoint for iOS users. Still, Apple’s not reinventing MacOS around touch controls, nor is it deviating from a traditional clamshell design. articles.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is Google’s second new frontier model this month
articles.content: Credit: Ryan McNeal / Android Authority TL;DR Google has introduced its latest frontier model — Gemini 4 Carbon. Carbon improves upon coding, agentic and scientific tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. However, cybersecurity is where it makes its biggest leap. The model initially will be released to a subset of cyber defenders before eventually rolling out to developers, businesses, and consumers. Carbon will be available at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off the input token price. About a month ago, Google teased us with its next frontier model — Gemini 4 Argon. Two weeks ago, that model saw the light of day as it finally rolled out for everyday users. While two weeks may not sound all that long, time moves a little faster in the world of AI. Google is now teasing us once again with a brand new frontier model. The latest AI model to come from the minds over there at the Mountain View-based firm is called Gemini 4 Carbon. According to Google , Carbon improves upon coding, agentic and scientific tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Carbon is said to outperform most other models, capturing the number one spot on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. However, cybersecurity is where Carbon really shines.
